fact: The first computer bug was a literal moth found inside the Harvard Mark II computer on September 9, 1947, taped into a logbook by operators working under Grace Hopper.
explanation: The term 'bug' for technical glitches predates this incident, but the moth gave the metaphor its most famous physical artifact.

fact: The name 'Wi-Fi' is not an acronym and stands for nothing; it was coined by branding firm Interbrand in 1999 as a play on 'Hi-Fi'.
explanation: The Wi-Fi Alliance briefly used the tagline 'The Standard for Wireless Fidelity' but later disowned it.

fact: The Apollo Guidance Computer that flew astronauts to the Moon had about 64 KB of memory and ran at 0.043 MHz.
explanation: A modern smartphone has roughly 100,000 times more processing power than the computer that landed Apollo 11.

fact: The term 'spam' for unwanted email comes from a 1970 Monty Python sketch in which the word 'Spam' is repeated more than 100 times.
explanation: Early Usenet users adopted the term in the 1980s to describe messages that drowned out conversation.

fact: The QWERTY keyboard layout was patented by Christopher Latham Sholes in 1878 and was designed for the Sholes and Glidden typewriter.
explanation: Common claims that QWERTY was designed to slow typists are disputed; it was more likely arranged to reduce jamming of adjacent typebars.

fact: The world's first webcam pointed at the Trojan Room coffee pot in the Cambridge University Computer Lab from 1991 to 2001.
explanation: Researchers built it so they could check whether the pot was full without walking down the hall.

fact: Bitcoin was introduced in a 2008 white paper authored by 'Satoshi Nakamoto', a pseudonym whose true identity has never been verified.
explanation: The genesis block mined on January 3, 2009 contained the headline 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.'

fact: The first email was sent by Ray Tomlinson in 1971 between two PDP-10 computers in the same room on ARPANET.
explanation: Tomlinson also chose the '@' symbol to separate the user name from the host name.

fact: Mariner 1 was destroyed shortly after its 1962 launch partly because of a missing hyphen in its guidance software.
explanation: Arthur C. Clarke later called it 'the most expensive hyphen in history.'

fact: The Therac-25 radiation therapy machine killed or seriously injured at least six patients between 1985 and 1987 due to a race condition in its software.
explanation: It became a standard case study in software engineering courses on safety-critical systems.

fact: Knight Capital lost about $440 million in 45 minutes on August 1, 2012 after deploying new trading software that activated dormant code.
explanation: The firm was effectively wiped out and was acquired by Getco a few months later.

fact: The Python programming language, released by Guido van Rossum in 1991, was named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake.
explanation: Many Python tutorials reference 'spam' and 'eggs' for the same reason.

fact: The first commercially available microprocessor, the Intel 4004, was released in 1971 and had 2,300 transistors.
explanation: Modern flagship CPUs and GPUs now contain tens of billions of transistors on a single die.

fact: The first iPhone, announced by Steve Jobs on January 9, 2007, did not support third-party apps; the App Store didn't launch until July 10, 2008.
explanation: Jobs initially wanted developers to build web apps for the iPhone instead of native apps.

fact: ARPANET sent its first message between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute on October 29, 1969; the system crashed after only the letters 'L' and 'O' were transmitted.
explanation: Programmer Charley Kline was trying to send the word 'LOGIN' when the remote host went down.

fact: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989 and made the technology freely available, with no patents and no royalties due.
explanation: CERN officially put the Web in the public domain on April 30, 1993.

fact: The world's first 1 GB hard drive, the IBM 3380, was introduced in 1980, weighed about 550 pounds, and cost roughly $40,000.
explanation: Today a 1 TB microSD card fits on a fingernail for under $100.

fact: Google was originally named 'BackRub' when Larry Page and Sergey Brin started it as a research project at Stanford in 1996.
explanation: They renamed it 'Google' in 1997, a play on the mathematical term 'googol' meaning 10^100.

fact: The domain Google.com was registered on September 15, 1997, and Google was incorporated a year later on September 4, 1998.
explanation: Its first office was a garage rented from Susan Wojcicki, later CEO of YouTube.

fact: Amazon.com sold its first book, Douglas Hofstadter's 'Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies', on July 16, 1995.
explanation: Founder Jeff Bezos had originally considered naming the company 'Cadabra'.

fact: The first hard disk drive, IBM's 1956 RAMAC 350, stored 5 MB of data on fifty 24-inch disks and weighed more than a ton.
explanation: It rented for about $3,200 per month, equivalent to over $35,000 today.

fact: The first text message ever sent, 'Merry Christmas,' was transmitted on December 3, 1992 by engineer Neil Papworth to Vodafone director Richard Jarvis.
explanation: Jarvis received it on an Orbitel 901 handset because phones at the time couldn't yet send SMS.

fact: The first commercial mobile phone, the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, went on sale in 1983 for $3,995 and offered 30 minutes of talk time per charge.
explanation: Engineer Martin Cooper had placed the first public handheld cellular call a decade earlier in 1973.

fact: The original Macintosh, released by Apple on January 24, 1984, shipped with 128 KB of RAM and a 9-inch monochrome screen.
explanation: It was the first mass-market computer with a graphical user interface and mouse.

fact: The Xerox Alto, built at Xerox PARC in 1973, was the first computer to use a graphical user interface, a mouse, and Ethernet networking.
explanation: Steve Jobs famously toured PARC in 1979 and adopted many of its ideas for the Lisa and Macintosh.

fact: Ethernet was invented by Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs at Xerox PARC in 1973 and originally ran at 2.94 Mbit/s.
explanation: Metcalfe later founded 3Com and formulated Metcalfe's Law about network value.

fact: The mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart at SRI in 1964 and patented in 1970 as an 'X-Y position indicator for a display system'.
explanation: Engelbart famously unveiled it during 1968's 'Mother of All Demos,' which also showcased hypertext and video conferencing.

fact: USB was developed by a group led by Ajay Bhatt at Intel and introduced commercially in 1996 as USB 1.0.
explanation: Despite popular belief, Bhatt did not receive royalties; he was a salaried Intel engineer.

fact: The HTTP protocol that powers the web was originally defined in 1991 with a single method, GET, by Tim Berners-Lee.
explanation: Today's HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 standards include multiplexing and use over UDP, but still expose the original GET semantics.

fact: The first banner ad on the web ran on HotWired.com on October 27, 1994, and was paid for by AT&T.
explanation: It reportedly had a click-through rate of 44%, far higher than modern banner ads.

fact: The Y2K problem stemmed from decades of representing years with only two digits to save storage space.
explanation: Governments and corporations spent an estimated $300-600 billion globally to remediate code before January 1, 2000.

fact: The first webpage was published by Tim Berners-Lee on August 6, 1991 at info.cern.ch and explained how the World Wide Web worked.
explanation: CERN restored a copy of the original page in 2013 at its original URL.

fact: The first computer virus to infect personal computers in the wild, Brain, was created in 1986 by brothers Basit and Amjad Farooq Alvi in Lahore, Pakistan.
explanation: It included the brothers' real names, address, and phone numbers in its code.

fact: The Morris Worm, released on November 2, 1988, infected an estimated 10% of internet-connected computers and was created by Cornell student Robert Tappan Morris.
explanation: Morris became the first person convicted under the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

fact: Linus Torvalds released the first version of the Linux kernel on September 17, 1991, when he was a 21-year-old student in Helsinki.
explanation: His original announcement on Usenet described it as 'just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu.'

fact: GNU was launched by Richard Stallman in 1983 with the goal of creating a complete free Unix-like operating system.
explanation: The name is a recursive acronym: 'GNU's Not Unix.'

fact: JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 10 days in May 1995, originally named Mocha and then LiveScript.
explanation: It was renamed JavaScript as a marketing move to leverage Java's popularity, despite the languages being unrelated.

fact: The first version of Microsoft Windows, Windows 1.0, was released on November 20, 1985 as a graphical operating environment on top of MS-DOS.
explanation: It required at least 256 KB of RAM and two double-sided floppy disk drives.

fact: Apple's Lisa, released in 1983 for $9,995, was the first commercial personal computer with a graphical user interface.
explanation: Steve Jobs was pushed off the Lisa team and joined the smaller Macintosh project instead.

fact: The IBM PC, released on August 12, 1981, used an open architecture that allowed third parties to clone it, ultimately commoditizing the PC market.
explanation: Compaq released the first fully compatible IBM PC clone in 1983 after reverse-engineering the BIOS.

fact: Microsoft was founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen on April 4, 1975 in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to write BASIC for the Altair 8800.
explanation: The company moved to Bellevue, Washington in 1979 and later to its current Redmond campus in 1986.

fact: Apple was founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne on April 1, 1976; Wayne sold his 10% stake 12 days later for $800.
explanation: That stake would later have been worth tens of billions of dollars.

fact: The Altair 8800, released in 1975 by MITS, is generally considered the first commercially successful personal computer.
explanation: It was sold as a kit through Popular Electronics magazine for $439.

fact: Moore's Law, proposed in a 1965 paper by Gordon Moore, originally predicted that the number of components on integrated circuits would double every year.
explanation: Moore revised the doubling period to roughly every two years in 1975.

fact: The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley, who later shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
explanation: The first working point-contact transistor was demonstrated on December 23, 1947.

fact: The integrated circuit was independently invented by Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments in 1958 and by Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959.
explanation: Kilby received the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics; Noyce had died in 1990.

fact: The IBM System/360, announced on April 7, 1964, was the first family of computers designed to share software across multiple price and performance levels.
explanation: IBM invested about $5 billion in its development, more than the Manhattan Project in adjusted dollars.

fact: The DEC PDP-1, introduced in 1959, was the platform for one of the earliest video games, Spacewar!, written by Steve Russell and others at MIT in 1962.
explanation: Only 53 PDP-1s were ever made, but its design heavily influenced minicomputers and Unix.

fact: Unix was created by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1969 on a DEC PDP-7.
explanation: Thompson reportedly wrote much of the initial system over a three-week period while his family was on vacation.

fact: The C programming language was developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs between 1969 and 1973, primarily to rewrite Unix.
explanation: The 1978 book by Kernighan and Ritchie became known simply as 'K&R'.

fact: Google's search engine handles roughly 8.5 billion queries per day, equivalent to about 100,000 per second.
explanation: It serves results from an index that comprises hundreds of billions of webpages.

fact: The first SMS text message was 160 characters long because German engineer Friedhelm Hillebrand determined in 1985 that this length was enough for most messages.
explanation: He tested it by typing random thoughts on a typewriter and counting characters.

fact: The first 'cell phone' call was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on April 3, 1973 to Joel Engel at rival Bell Labs.
explanation: Cooper's prototype DynaTAC weighed about 2.4 pounds and took 10 hours to recharge.

fact: The very first commercial cellular network launched in Tokyo on December 3, 1979, operated by NTT.
explanation: The U.S. did not get its first commercial cellular service until October 1983 in Chicago.

fact: Bluetooth is named after 10th-century Danish king Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson, who unified parts of Denmark and Norway.
explanation: The Bluetooth logo is a bind rune merging Harald's initials in Younger Futhark.

fact: The first publicly accessible website in the United States went online at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center on December 12, 1991.
explanation: SLAC physicist Paul Kunz set up the site after meeting Tim Berners-Lee at CERN earlier that year.

fact: The first emoticon, ':-)', was proposed by computer scientist Scott Fahlman on a Carnegie Mellon bulletin board on September 19, 1982.
explanation: He suggested it to mark posts that were not meant to be taken seriously.

fact: The first emoji set was created by NTT DoCoMo's Shigetaka Kurita in 1999 and consisted of 176 12x12 pixel images.
explanation: The Museum of Modern Art in New York acquired the original set for its permanent collection in 2016.

fact: Facebook was launched as 'TheFacebook' on February 4, 2004 from a Harvard dorm room by Mark Zuckerberg and four classmates.
explanation: It dropped 'The' in 2005 after acquiring the domain facebook.com for $200,000.

fact: Twitter was launched on March 21, 2006, when Jack Dorsey posted the first tweet: 'just setting up my twttr.'
explanation: That tweet was later sold as an NFT for about $2.9 million in March 2021.

fact: YouTube was founded on February 14, 2005, and the first video, 'Me at the zoo', was uploaded by co-founder Jawed Karim on April 23, 2005.
explanation: The 19-second clip was filmed at the San Diego Zoo and remains online.

fact: WhatsApp was bought by Facebook for about $19 billion in 2014, at which point the company had only 55 employees.
explanation: Co-founder Jan Koum signed the deal on the door of the welfare office where he once collected food stamps.

fact: Instagram had only 13 employees when Facebook acquired it for about $1 billion in April 2012.
explanation: The app had launched just 19 months earlier on October 6, 2010.

fact: Snapchat's parent company turned down a $3 billion all-cash offer from Facebook in 2013, when founder Evan Spiegel was 23 years old.
explanation: Snap Inc. went public in 2017 at a valuation of about $24 billion.

fact: PageRank, the algorithm at the heart of early Google search, was developed at Stanford and named after co-founder Larry Page.
explanation: The original Stanford patent for PageRank was assigned to the university and licensed exclusively to Google.

fact: Wikipedia launched on January 15, 2001, as a complement to the more formal Nupedia, but quickly surpassed it.
explanation: It is written in over 300 languages and run by the nonprofit Wikimedia Foundation.

fact: The first version of Adobe Photoshop, released in February 1990, was developed by brothers Thomas and John Knoll.
explanation: It originally ran only on Macintosh and was distributed on floppy disks.

fact: Internet Explorer 6, released in 2001, remained Microsoft's flagship browser for over five years and at its peak held more than 80% of the browser market.
explanation: Its many security issues and slow update cycle helped drive the rise of Firefox and Chrome.

fact: Google Chrome was released on September 2, 2008 and surpassed Internet Explorer in global usage by 2012.
explanation: Chrome's open-source base, Chromium, now also powers Microsoft Edge, Opera, and Brave.

fact: The Firefox web browser was first released by the Mozilla Foundation on November 9, 2004, after the open-sourcing of Netscape's code in 1998.
explanation: The 1.0 launch was funded in part by a two-page community ad in The New York Times.

fact: Yahoo! was founded by Jerry Yang and David Filo at Stanford in 1994 and originally called 'Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web.'
explanation: Yahoo declined to buy Google for $1 million in 1998 and Facebook for $1 billion in 2006.

fact: The original IBM PC's BIOS chip was just 8 KB and was reverse-engineered legally by Compaq using a clean-room development process.
explanation: Compaq's clone gave rise to the entire PC clone industry that ran on Intel chips and DOS.

fact: MS-DOS was originally based on 86-DOS, also called QDOS ('Quick and Dirty Operating System'), which Microsoft bought from Seattle Computer Products for $75,000 in 1981.
explanation: Microsoft then licensed it to IBM for the IBM PC while retaining the right to sell it to others.

fact: The original Game Boy, released by Nintendo in 1989, used an 8-bit Sharp processor and a 4-color green LCD screen.
explanation: It sold over 118 million units across all variants, making it one of the best-selling handhelds ever.

fact: Pong, released by Atari in 1972, was one of the earliest commercially successful video games and was designed by Allan Alcorn as a training exercise.
explanation: Its prototype was so popular that the original cabinet broke from too many quarters jammed into the coin slot.

fact: The Nintendo Entertainment System, released in North America in 1985, helped revive the U.S. video game market after the 1983 crash.
explanation: Its packaging as a 'toy' helped get it onto store shelves that had banned 'video games.'

fact: The PlayStation began as a 1988 partnership between Sony and Nintendo to make a CD-ROM add-on for the SNES, which Nintendo abruptly canceled.
explanation: Sony went on to release its own PlayStation in 1994, eventually selling more than 102 million units.

fact: The first commercial DVD player was released in Japan by Toshiba in November 1996, with U.S. release in March 1997.
explanation: DVDs could initially store about 4.7 GB on a single layer, compared to 700 MB on a CD.

fact: Compact Discs were jointly developed by Sony and Philips, and the first commercial CD pressed was ABBA's 'The Visitors' in August 1982.
explanation: CDs were designed to hold 74 minutes of audio, reportedly to fit Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.

fact: The MP3 format was developed primarily by Karlheinz Brandenburg and colleagues at Germany's Fraunhofer Institute and standardized in 1993.
explanation: Test tracks like Suzanne Vega's 'Tom's Diner' were used to fine-tune the perceptual audio coding.

fact: Napster, the file-sharing service co-created by Shawn Fanning in 1999, was shut down by court order in 2001 after losing copyright cases.
explanation: At its peak, it had about 80 million registered users.

fact: The original Sony Walkman, the TPS-L2, was launched in Japan on July 1, 1979 and helped popularize personal portable music.
explanation: Sony made it after co-founder Masaru Ibuka asked for a way to listen to operas on long flights.

fact: Apple's iPod, introduced on October 23, 2001, originally held 1,000 songs on a 5 GB hard drive and used a mechanical scroll wheel.
explanation: Steve Jobs unveiled it with the line '1,000 songs in your pocket.'

fact: Steve Wozniak single-handedly designed the Apple I and Apple II computers, including their motherboards and operating systems.
explanation: He has said he insisted on selling the Apple I rather than giving it away only because Steve Jobs convinced him.

fact: The first home computer mouse to be widely sold was Apple's mouse for the Lisa in 1983, manufactured by Logitech precursor Hovey-Kelley.
explanation: Engelbart's earlier prototypes had used wheels rather than a ball.

fact: The PostScript page description language, released by Adobe in 1984, made the desktop publishing revolution possible by giving printers a common vector language.
explanation: Adobe's first major customer was Apple, which licensed PostScript for the LaserWriter printer.

fact: The PDF format was created at Adobe by John Warnock in 1991 and released publicly in 1993.
explanation: It became an open ISO standard (ISO 32000-1) in 2008.

fact: The PGP email encryption program, created by Phil Zimmermann in 1991, became the subject of a U.S. criminal investigation for violating export controls on cryptography.
explanation: Zimmermann's lawyers cleverly published the source code as a book, since books were protected by the First Amendment.

fact: The Data Encryption Standard (DES) was adopted by the U.S. government in 1977 and used a 56-bit key, which became insecure as computing power grew.
explanation: DES was officially replaced by the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in 2001.

fact: The RSA public-key cryptosystem was published in 1977 by Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman at MIT.
explanation: British cryptographer Clifford Cocks had independently invented a similar scheme at GCHQ in 1973 but it was classified until 1997.

fact: The first public demonstration of public-key cryptography was in a 1976 paper by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography.'
explanation: They received the 2015 Turing Award for the work.

fact: Tor, a system for anonymous internet communication, was originally developed by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory starting in the mid-1990s.
explanation: Its name stands for 'The Onion Router,' referring to its layered encryption.

fact: The first version of TCP/IP was specified in 1974 in a paper by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn titled 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication.'
explanation: The full IPv4 standard was published in 1981 in RFC 791.

fact: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, while IPv6 has roughly 3.4 x 10^38, enough to assign trillions of addresses to every square millimeter of the Earth's surface.
explanation: IPv4 address exhaustion was officially reached by IANA in February 2011.

fact: DNS, the system that translates names like google.com into IP addresses, was designed by Paul Mockapetris in 1983 and specified in RFC 882 and 883.
explanation: Before DNS, every internet-connected computer downloaded a single hosts.txt file maintained at SRI.

fact: The first registered .com domain was Symbolics.com, registered on March 15, 1985 by Symbolics, Inc., a computer company.
explanation: It was later sold to investors in 2009 in a deal whose price was never officially disclosed.

fact: Email predates the World Wide Web by about two decades; ARPANET email had largely standardized on its @-based format by the early 1970s.
explanation: By 1973, an ARPANET study found that 75% of all network traffic was email.

fact: The first commercial spam email is generally credited to a 1978 message sent by Gary Thuerk of DEC to about 400 ARPANET users.
explanation: It advertised a new DEC computer and reportedly generated about $13 million in sales.

fact: The first GIF format was introduced by CompuServe on June 15, 1987 to provide color images that could be transmitted over slow modems.
explanation: Its compression scheme, LZW, was later subject to a famous patent dispute in the 1990s.

fact: The JPEG image format was first standardized in 1992 by the Joint Photographic Experts Group, after work begun in 1986.
explanation: JPEG's perceptual compression discards high-frequency detail the human eye is less sensitive to.

fact: PNG was developed in 1995 as a free alternative to GIF, partly to avoid LZW patent fees.
explanation: The recursive joke is that PNG stands for 'PNG's Not GIF'.

fact: The first version of the Android operating system was released by Google on September 23, 2008 with the HTC Dream (T-Mobile G1).
explanation: Google had bought Android Inc., founded by Andy Rubin, in 2005 for an undisclosed sum widely reported at about $50 million.

fact: iOS was originally called 'iPhone OS' when introduced with the first iPhone in 2007, and Apple renamed it iOS in June 2010.
explanation: The name change reflected its expansion to the iPad and iPod touch.

fact: The Raspberry Pi, a credit-card-sized computer designed for education, launched on February 29, 2012 and sold out within hours.
explanation: More than 50 million units have been sold across all models.

fact: The Arduino microcontroller platform was created in 2005 at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea in Italy to give designers an easy way to prototype electronics.
explanation: Its open-source hardware design has spawned countless compatible boards.

fact: The first cell tower in the United States went into commercial service in Chicago on October 13, 1983.
explanation: It was operated by Ameritech Mobile Communications, an AT&T spinoff.

fact: Cellular networks are called 'cellular' because coverage areas are divided into geographic 'cells', each served by a low-power base station.
explanation: The cellular concept was developed at Bell Labs in 1947 but not deployed commercially until the 1980s.

fact: The GSM mobile phone standard was first deployed by Radiolinja in Finland in 1991.
explanation: GSM now serves billions of subscribers across more than 200 countries.

fact: The first SIM card was introduced by Munich-based Giesecke & Devrient in 1991 and was the size of a credit card.
explanation: Modern eSIMs eliminate the physical card entirely and are programmable over the air.

fact: GPS achieved full operational capability on April 27, 1995 with a constellation of 24 satellites operated by the U.S. Department of Defense.
explanation: Civilian access was deliberately degraded by 'Selective Availability' until President Clinton ordered it turned off on May 1, 2000.

fact: Each GPS satellite carries multiple atomic clocks accurate to within a few nanoseconds, essential for precise position calculations.
explanation: Relativistic effects must be accounted for; without correction, GPS errors would accumulate at about 10 km per day.

fact: The first satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957 and broadcast simple radio beeps at 20 and 40 MHz.
explanation: It triggered the 'space race' and led to the U.S. founding of NASA in 1958 and ARPA (later DARPA) in 1958.

fact: ARPA, the agency that funded the development of ARPANET, was founded by President Eisenhower in February 1958 in response to Sputnik.
explanation: It was renamed DARPA in 1972 to emphasize its 'Defense' focus.

fact: The Cisco brand name comes from 'San Francisco' and the company's logo represents the Golden Gate Bridge.
explanation: Cisco was founded by Stanford computer scientists Leonard Bosack and Sandy Lerner in 1984.

fact: Oracle Corporation, founded in 1977, is named after a CIA project nicknamed 'Oracle' that early Oracle founders had worked on.
explanation: Founders Larry Ellison, Bob Miner, and Ed Oates started the company as Software Development Laboratories.

fact: Intel was founded in 1968 by Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce, who left Fairchild Semiconductor with venture capitalist Arthur Rock.
explanation: The name is a contraction of 'Integrated Electronics.'

fact: AMD was founded in 1969 by Jerry Sanders and seven colleagues who had also left Fairchild Semiconductor.
explanation: Sanders famously said 'people first, products and profits will follow.'

fact: NVIDIA was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem in a Denny's diner in San Jose.
explanation: Its first major hit was the RIVA 128 graphics chip in 1997.

fact: The GPU as we know it was popularized by NVIDIA's 1999 GeForce 256, which Nvidia marketed as 'the world's first GPU.'
explanation: Programmable shaders, introduced in the GeForce 3 in 2001, opened the door to general-purpose GPU computing.

fact: CUDA, NVIDIA's parallel computing platform for GPUs, was first released in 2007 and is widely used for deep learning today.
explanation: It allows developers to use C-like code to run massively parallel computations on GPUs.

fact: The first deep learning system to win the ImageNet large-scale visual recognition challenge was AlexNet in 2012.
explanation: Created by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton, it dropped the error rate by about 10 percentage points and helped trigger the modern AI boom.

fact: IBM's Deep Blue defeated reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in May 1997.
explanation: Deep Blue could evaluate roughly 200 million chess positions per second.

fact: IBM's Watson won Jeopardy! in February 2011, defeating champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter over three episodes.
explanation: Watson ran on 90 IBM Power 750 servers with 16 terabytes of RAM.

fact: DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated Go world champion Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016.
explanation: Go has more legal board positions than there are atoms in the observable universe.

fact: AlphaGo Zero, a 2017 successor, learned to play Go entirely from self-play and reached superhuman performance in 40 days.
explanation: It surpassed the version that defeated Lee Sedol after only three days of training.

fact: GPT-3 was released by OpenAI in 2020 and had 175 billion parameters, more than 100x its predecessor GPT-2.
explanation: It demonstrated that scaling language models alone could yield surprising new capabilities.

fact: ChatGPT was launched by OpenAI on November 30, 2022 and reached 100 million monthly users in two months, the fastest growth then recorded.
explanation: It was initially built on GPT-3.5, an instruction-tuned variant of GPT-3.

fact: The Turing Test was proposed by Alan Turing in his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', published in the journal Mind.
explanation: Turing called the original setup 'the imitation game.'

fact: The first chatbot, ELIZA, was created by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT between 1964 and 1966 and simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist.
explanation: Weizenbaum was disturbed by how readily people attributed understanding to such a simple program.

fact: The Turing Award, often called the 'Nobel Prize of Computing', has been given out by the ACM since 1966.
explanation: Today it carries a $1 million prize funded by Google.

fact: Alan Turing was prosecuted for homosexuality in the UK in 1952 and chemically castrated; he died from cyanide poisoning in 1954.
explanation: He was granted a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.

fact: Ada Lovelace wrote what is widely considered the first algorithm intended for execution by a machine, in 1843 notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.
explanation: The U.S. Department of Defense named a programming language 'Ada' after her in 1980.

fact: Babbage's Analytical Engine was a mechanical general-purpose computer designed in the 1830s but never fully built.
explanation: Modern reconstructions of his earlier Difference Engine work according to his original plans.

fact: The 'Bombe' machine designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman at Bletchley Park helped break the German Enigma code during World War II.
explanation: Some historians estimate the work shortened the war by up to two years and saved millions of lives.

fact: The Colossus, built at Bletchley Park during WWII, was the world's first programmable electronic digital computer.
explanation: Its existence remained classified by the British government for decades.

fact: ENIAC, completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania, weighed about 30 tons and contained about 17,468 vacuum tubes.
explanation: It was used to compute artillery firing tables and contributed to early hydrogen bomb calculations.

fact: The term 'computer' originally referred to people, often women, who performed calculations by hand.
explanation: Many of the ENIAC's first 'programmers' were women who had been human computers, like Kay McNulty and Jean Bartik.

fact: COBOL, developed in 1959, was largely designed by Grace Hopper and a committee with the goal of being readable like English.
explanation: An estimated 200 billion lines of COBOL code are still in active use today, mostly in banking and government.

fact: FORTRAN, released by IBM in 1957, was the first widely used high-level programming language and is still used in scientific computing.
explanation: Its name is short for 'FORmula TRANslation'.

fact: BASIC was developed at Dartmouth in 1964 by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz to make programming accessible to non-technical students.
explanation: Microsoft's first product was a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800.

fact: Pascal was designed by Niklaus Wirth in 1970 and was popularized at universities for teaching structured programming.
explanation: Turbo Pascal, released by Borland in 1983 for $49.95, became a defining tool for a generation of programmers.

fact: C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs starting in 1979, originally as 'C with Classes.'
explanation: It was renamed C++ in 1983, a play on the '++' increment operator in C.

fact: Java, released by Sun Microsystems in 1995, was originally named 'Oak' after a tree outside James Gosling's office.
explanation: Its 'write once, run anywhere' promise relied on the Java Virtual Machine.

fact: Ruby was created by Yukihiro 'Matz' Matsumoto in Japan and first released in 1995.
explanation: Ruby on Rails, released in 2004, popularized Ruby globally and helped shape modern web frameworks.

fact: PHP was created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as a set of 'Personal Home Page Tools' written in C.
explanation: It now powers a large share of web servers, including the original Facebook.

fact: Perl was developed by Larry Wall in 1987 and became known as the 'Swiss Army chainsaw' of scripting languages.
explanation: Wall once described Perl as designed to make 'easy things easy and hard things possible.'

fact: The Rust programming language was created by Graydon Hoare starting in 2006 and sponsored by Mozilla starting in 2009.
explanation: It hit 1.0 in 2015 and has since been adopted in the Linux kernel.

fact: Go was designed at Google by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson and announced in November 2009.
explanation: Its mascot is a gopher designed by illustrator Renée French.

fact: TypeScript was created at Microsoft by Anders Hejlsberg and first released in October 2012.
explanation: Hejlsberg also led the design of Turbo Pascal, Delphi, and C#.

fact: C# was designed at Microsoft by Anders Hejlsberg and released in 2000 alongside the .NET framework.
explanation: Its name follows musical notation where '#' indicates a raised pitch.

fact: Lisp, created by John McCarthy in 1958, is the second-oldest high-level programming language still in widespread use after Fortran.
explanation: Its syntax is based on parenthesized lists, leading to jokes about 'lots of irritating superfluous parentheses.'

fact: Smalltalk, developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s by Alan Kay's team, is one of the earliest fully object-oriented languages.
explanation: Its ideas influenced Objective-C, Java, Python, and Ruby.

fact: The 'object-oriented programming' paradigm and the term itself were coined by Alan Kay in the late 1960s and 1970s.
explanation: Kay later said the term focused too much on objects and not enough on messaging.

fact: Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage Linux kernel development after the previous tool, BitKeeper, became non-free.
explanation: Torvalds reportedly wrote the initial version over the course of about a week.

fact: GitHub was founded in 2008 by Tom Preston-Werner, Chris Wanstrath, P. J. Hyett, and Scott Chacon, and Microsoft acquired it in 2018 for $7.5 billion.
explanation: GitHub hosts more than 100 million developer accounts.

fact: Stack Overflow was launched on September 15, 2008 by Jeff Atwood and Joel Spolsky as an open Q&A site for programmers.
explanation: It became part of the Stack Exchange Network of more than 170 Q&A communities.

fact: The hashtag was first proposed for Twitter by Chris Messina in a tweet on August 23, 2007.
explanation: Twitter formally adopted hashtags as clickable links in 2009.

fact: Skype was launched in August 2003 by Janus Friis, Niklas Zennström and Estonian developers, and was acquired by Microsoft in 2011 for $8.5 billion.
explanation: Microsoft announced in 2025 that it would retire Skype in favor of Microsoft Teams.

fact: Zoom Video Communications was founded in 2011 by Eric Yuan, who had been a vice president at Cisco WebEx.
explanation: Daily active participants on Zoom grew from about 10 million to over 300 million during the early COVID-19 pandemic.

fact: The first commercial computer mouse to ship with a personal computer was the Star, a Xerox 8010 system released in 1981.
explanation: The Xerox Star pioneered many concepts later popularized by Macintosh and Windows.

fact: The first 'killer app' for personal computers is widely credited to VisiCalc, a 1979 spreadsheet by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston for the Apple II.
explanation: Lotus 1-2-3 overtook it in the IBM PC market within a few years.

fact: The first widely used database system, IBM's IMS, was developed for the Apollo program to track parts for the Saturn V rocket.
explanation: IMS remains in commercial use over 50 years later.

fact: The relational database model was proposed by Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper while he was working at IBM Research.
explanation: Codd received the Turing Award in 1981 for the work.

fact: SQL was developed at IBM in the 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce; the language was originally called SEQUEL.
explanation: It was renamed SQL due to a trademark conflict with the UK-based Hawker Siddeley aircraft company.

fact: MySQL was first released in 1995 by Swedish founders Michael Widenius, David Axmark, and Allan Larsson.
explanation: Sun Microsystems bought MySQL AB in 2008 for $1 billion, and Oracle later acquired Sun in 2010.

fact: MongoDB, released in 2009, popularized the document-oriented 'NoSQL' database paradigm.
explanation: Its name comes from 'humongous,' reflecting its design for large data sets.

fact: Redis, an in-memory data store, was created by Salvatore Sanfilippo in 2009 to solve scaling problems for a real-time analytics startup.
explanation: Its name is short for 'REmote DIctionary Server.'

fact: Linux now runs on the vast majority of internet servers, all of the world's top 500 supercomputers, and Android phones at the kernel level.
explanation: Microsoft, once Linux's biggest corporate critic, is now one of the largest contributors to the Linux kernel.

fact: Apache, first released in 1995, was for many years the most widely used web server on the internet.
explanation: Its name was originally said to be a pun on 'a patchy server' built from patches to the NCSA HTTPd code.

fact: Nginx was created by Russian developer Igor Sysoev in 2004 to solve the C10k problem of handling 10,000 concurrent connections.
explanation: Its name is pronounced 'engine x' and it is widely used as a reverse proxy and load balancer.

fact: The 'cloud' in cloud computing is named after the cloud symbol used to represent abstracted networks in old engineering diagrams.
explanation: Amazon's S3 service launched in March 2006, often cited as a milestone in modern public cloud computing.

fact: Amazon Web Services started by offering Simple Queue Service in 2004, followed by S3 in 2006 and EC2 in 2006.
explanation: AWS now generates a substantial portion of Amazon's overall operating profit.

fact: Salesforce was founded by Marc Benioff and three co-founders in 1999 as one of the first major SaaS companies.
explanation: Its early 'No Software' marketing campaign emphasized cloud-based delivery.

fact: Slack was launched in August 2013 by Stewart Butterfield and others; the company had previously tried and failed to make a game called Glitch.
explanation: Salesforce acquired Slack in 2021 for about $27.7 billion.

fact: GitHub Copilot, an AI pair programmer based on OpenAI Codex, was announced by GitHub on June 29, 2021.
explanation: It is trained largely on publicly available source code from GitHub.

fact: The OpenAI organization was founded in December 2015 by figures including Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Ilya Sutskever, initially as a nonprofit.
explanation: OpenAI created a 'capped profit' subsidiary, OpenAI LP, in 2019 to enable large-scale investment.

fact: The first transatlantic telegraph cable was completed in 1858, but failed within weeks; a permanent cable came in 1866.
explanation: It cut the time for a message between London and New York from about 10 days to a few minutes.

fact: Alexander Graham Bell was granted a U.S. patent for the telephone on March 7, 1876, narrowly beating Elisha Gray, who filed a caveat the same day.
explanation: Bell's first successful test came three days later when he said 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'

fact: Guglielmo Marconi transmitted the first transatlantic radio signal on December 12, 1901, sending the letter 'S' in Morse code from Cornwall to Newfoundland.
explanation: Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun.

fact: Television was first publicly demonstrated by John Logie Baird in London on January 26, 1926.
explanation: Baird's mechanical system was later superseded by all-electronic television developed by Philo Farnsworth and Vladimir Zworykin.

fact: The first regular high-definition television service was launched by the BBC on November 2, 1936.
explanation: Broadcasts were suspended during WWII and resumed in 1946.

fact: Color television was first commercially broadcast in the United States by CBS in 1951, although the system was incompatible with existing black-and-white sets.
explanation: NBC's compatible NTSC standard was adopted in 1953 and became the U.S. norm for decades.

fact: The fax machine concept was patented by Scottish inventor Alexander Bain in 1843, predating the telephone by over 30 years.
explanation: Commercial fax services like the Belinographe operated as early as the late 1800s for newspaper photo transmission.

fact: The first laser was demonstrated by Theodore Maiman at Hughes Research Laboratories on May 16, 1960 using a synthetic ruby.
explanation: The acronym stands for 'Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.'

fact: The first fiber-optic communication system was deployed for telephone service in 1977 by AT&T in Chicago and GTE in Long Beach.
explanation: Modern submarine fiber-optic cables can carry hundreds of terabits per second across an ocean.

fact: The first transatlantic fiber-optic cable, TAT-8, entered service in 1988 with a capacity of about 280 megabits per second.
explanation: Recent transatlantic cables exceed 200 terabits per second per cable.

fact: The world's longest undersea cable, SEA-ME-WE 3, runs more than 39,000 kilometers from Germany to Australia.
explanation: Roughly 99% of intercontinental internet traffic travels through undersea cables, not satellites.

fact: The first geostationary communications satellite, Syncom 3, was launched in 1964 and broadcast that year's Tokyo Olympics across the Pacific.
explanation: Geostationary orbits sit at about 35,786 km altitude over the equator.

fact: The Iridium satellite phone system, originally planned with 77 satellites (hence the name after element 77), launched commercial service in 1998.
explanation: It went bankrupt the next year but was bought out and continues to operate today with 66 satellites.

fact: SpaceX's Starlink began launching satellites in 2019 and has deployed more than 6,000 by 2024, the largest constellation in history.
explanation: Starlink provides broadband internet to over 100 countries from low Earth orbit.

fact: The first car phone services were 'mobile telephone systems' that began in 1946 in St. Louis using AT&T's MTS technology.
explanation: Capacity was tiny - only three radio channels initially served the entire city.

fact: The Sony Trinitron color TV, introduced in 1968, used a unique aperture grille design and won an Emmy Award for engineering excellence in 1973.
explanation: It dominated the high-end TV market for decades until LCDs took over.

fact: VHS won the home video format war against Betamax during the late 1970s and early 1980s, despite Betamax often offering better image quality.
explanation: VHS's longer recording time, especially for full-length movies and sports, was a key factor.

fact: The Blu-ray Disc format defeated HD DVD in a 2008 format war when Warner Bros. announced it would back only Blu-ray.
explanation: Sony's PlayStation 3, which included a Blu-ray drive, was decisive in establishing the format.

fact: The 3.5-inch floppy disk standard held 1.44 MB, was introduced by Sony in 1982, and dominated until USB drives replaced it.
explanation: The 'Save' icon in many programs is still a stylized floppy disk.

fact: ZIP files were invented by Phil Katz, founder of PKWARE, and the format was first publicly described in 1989.
explanation: The ZIP specification has been intentionally open and unencumbered by patents.

fact: The Game Boy Tetris is one of the best-selling video games of all time, partly thanks to a bundling deal Nintendo struck with Russian creator Alexey Pajitnov.
explanation: Pajitnov, who first wrote Tetris in 1984, only began collecting royalties from his game after 1996.

fact: The 'Konami Code' (Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A) was created in 1986 by Konami developer Kazuhisa Hashimoto.
explanation: He invented it as a debugging shortcut for the game Gradius and forgot to remove it.

fact: Minecraft, created by Markus 'Notch' Persson and first released in 2009, became the best-selling video game of all time, surpassing 300 million copies sold.
explanation: Microsoft acquired Mojang and Minecraft in 2014 for $2.5 billion.

fact: World of Warcraft launched on November 23, 2004 and reached a peak of about 12 million subscribers in 2010.
explanation: It is generally credited with mainstreaming the massively multiplayer online role-playing genre.

fact: Fortnite's Battle Royale mode was launched in September 2017 as a free-to-play addition to the original cooperative game.
explanation: Within a year it had more than 200 million players and generated billions in revenue.

fact: Steam, Valve's digital game store, launched in September 2003 initially to distribute updates for Counter-Strike.
explanation: Today Steam regularly has tens of millions of concurrent users.

fact: Space Invaders, released by Taito in 1978, was so popular in Japan that it was widely rumored to have caused a temporary 100-yen coin shortage.
explanation: The shortage rumor is widely disputed by historians, but the game's revenue was staggering.

fact: Pac-Man, designed by Toru Iwatani at Namco and released in 1980, was inspired in part by a pizza with one slice missing.
explanation: Pac-Man's original Japanese name was Puck Man.

fact: The Magnavox Odyssey, released in 1972, was the first home video game console and was designed by Ralph Baer.
explanation: Atari paid Magnavox a settlement after Magnavox sued Atari claiming Pong infringed on Odyssey patents.

fact: Ralph Baer is often called the 'father of video games' for his 'Brown Box' prototype, demonstrated in 1968.
explanation: He received the U.S. National Medal of Technology in 2006.

fact: The Atari 2600, released in 1977, popularized the use of swappable game cartridges based on ROM chips.
explanation: By the time it was discontinued in 1992, it had sold roughly 30 million units.

fact: The video game crash of 1983 in North America wiped out billions of dollars in industry revenue, partly due to oversaturation and poor-quality games.
explanation: Atari's E.T. game, rushed to release in five weeks, became a symbol of the crash, and unsold copies were buried in a New Mexico landfill.

fact: Excavators in 2014 confirmed the long-rumored Atari E.T. landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, recovering thousands of buried game cartridges.
explanation: Some recovered cartridges later sold to collectors and museums.

fact: Adobe Flash, originally released as FutureSplash Animator in 1996, dominated web animation in the 2000s but was officially discontinued on December 31, 2020.
explanation: Steve Jobs's 2010 open letter 'Thoughts on Flash' accelerated its decline.

fact: HTML5 became an official W3C Recommendation on October 28, 2014 after years of development by the WHATWG and W3C.
explanation: It eliminated the need for plug-ins like Flash and Silverlight for most web video and animation.

fact: The original web browser, Mosaic, was released by NCSA in 1993 and popularized inline images on web pages.
explanation: Marc Andreessen, a Mosaic co-creator, later co-founded Netscape.

fact: Netscape Navigator went public on August 9, 1995, and its stock more than doubled on the first day, helping kick off the dot-com boom.
explanation: The company would later be acquired by AOL in 1998 for $4.2 billion in stock.

fact: AOL acquired Time Warner in 2000 in a $164 billion deal that quickly became known as one of the worst mergers in corporate history.
explanation: The combined company eventually wrote down nearly $99 billion in losses tied to the merger.

fact: Nokia 3310, released in 2000, sold about 126 million units and became a symbol of indestructible mobile phones.
explanation: It featured the famous mobile game 'Snake II'.

fact: BlackBerry, made by Canada's Research In Motion, popularized push email in 1999 and was famously called 'CrackBerry' by users addicted to its messaging.
explanation: President Barack Obama fought to keep his BlackBerry when he entered office in 2009.

fact: The Palm Pilot 1000, released in March 1996, sold a million units in its first 18 months and helped define the personal digital assistant category.
explanation: Its handwriting recognition system, Graffiti, required users to learn a simplified alphabet.

fact: Newton, Apple's 1993 PDA, popularized the term 'personal digital assistant' but was widely mocked for poor handwriting recognition.
explanation: It was discontinued by Steve Jobs in 1998 after his return to Apple.

fact: The first Bluetooth specification, version 1.0, was released by the Bluetooth Special Interest Group in 1999.
explanation: Founding members included Ericsson, Nokia, IBM, Intel, and Toshiba.

fact: Wi-Fi's underlying IEEE 802.11 standard was first released in 1997 at a maximum speed of 2 Mbit/s.
explanation: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be), ratified in 2024, can exceed 40 Gbit/s in ideal conditions.

fact: The maximum theoretical throughput of USB 1.0 was 12 Mbit/s, USB 2.0 was 480 Mbit/s, and USB 3.0 was 5 Gbit/s.
explanation: USB4, released in 2019, builds on the Thunderbolt 3 protocol and reaches 40 Gbit/s.

fact: Thunderbolt was originally co-developed by Intel and Apple under the codename 'Light Peak' and launched in the 2011 MacBook Pro.
explanation: Despite the name, current Thunderbolt uses copper cabling, not light.

fact: FireWire (IEEE 1394) was developed at Apple in the late 1980s and originally used to connect digital camcorders to computers.
explanation: Apple charged a $1-per-port royalty to other manufacturers, contributing to its decline against USB.

fact: The original IBM PC's 5 1/4-inch floppy disks held only 160 KB of data, less than a single modern email message.
explanation: Later double-sided, double-density versions raised capacity to 360 KB.

fact: The first commercial CD-ROM drive shipped in 1985 from Hitachi and Sony, with a price of about $1,000.
explanation: Early CD-ROMs could hold about 650 MB, more than 450 floppy disks of data.

fact: Encarta, Microsoft's digital encyclopedia, was launched in 1993 on CD-ROM and was discontinued in 2009 because of competition from Wikipedia.
explanation: It was based largely on content licensed from the older Funk & Wagnalls Encyclopedia.

fact: The Encyclopaedia Britannica printed its final paper edition in 2010, after 244 years of continuous print publication.
explanation: It now exists only online, in part due to digital competition.

fact: Project Gutenberg, started by Michael Hart at the University of Illinois in 1971, is the oldest digital library of public domain books.
explanation: Its first text was the U.S. Declaration of Independence, typed in all capitals.

fact: The Internet Archive, founded by Brewster Kahle in 1996, runs the Wayback Machine, which holds hundreds of billions of archived web pages.
explanation: Its headquarters is housed in a former Christian Science church in San Francisco.

fact: Wayback Machine users can view captures of webpages going back to the mid-1990s.
explanation: It indexes captures by URL and date, allowing users to browse the historical web.

fact: The Stuxnet computer worm, discovered in 2010, targeted Iranian nuclear centrifuges and is widely attributed to a joint U.S.-Israeli operation.
explanation: It is considered the first known cyberweapon to cause physical damage to industrial equipment.

fact: The 'ILOVEYOU' worm, released on May 5, 2000 by a Filipino student, infected more than 10 million Windows computers within days.
explanation: It spread by sending itself as an email attachment with the subject 'ILOVEYOU' and the file 'LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.txt.vbs'.

fact: The 'Heartbleed' bug, disclosed in April 2014, affected OpenSSL and exposed memory contents of perhaps two-thirds of internet servers.
explanation: It was caused by a missing bounds check on a heartbeat extension to the TLS protocol.

fact: The 'Log4Shell' vulnerability disclosed in December 2021 in the Log4j Java library was considered one of the most serious internet bugs in years.
explanation: U.S. CISA Director Jen Easterly called it 'one of the most serious I've seen in my entire career, if not the most serious.'

fact: The 2017 Equifax data breach exposed sensitive information on about 147 million Americans, partly due to an unpatched Apache Struts flaw.
explanation: Equifax paid at least $700 million in penalties and consumer compensation.

fact: The 2017 WannaCry ransomware outbreak infected more than 200,000 computers in over 150 countries within days.
explanation: It was halted in part when researcher Marcus Hutchins registered a domain referenced in the code as a 'kill switch.'

fact: Bitcoin's blockchain produces a new block roughly every 10 minutes, with the protocol adjusting difficulty every 2,016 blocks.
explanation: The total supply is capped at 21 million bitcoins, expected to be reached around the year 2140.

fact: Ethereum was conceived by Vitalik Buterin in 2013 and launched as a public blockchain on July 30, 2015.
explanation: It introduced 'smart contracts' executed by the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

fact: On May 22, 2010, programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas in what became known as 'Bitcoin Pizza Day.'
explanation: At later peak bitcoin prices, those 10,000 BTC would have been worth more than $600 million.

fact: Domino's Pizza took the world's first online pizza order in 1994 in Santa Cruz, California.
explanation: Pizza Hut had also experimented with online ordering on its 'PizzaNet' system in 1994.

fact: Amazon's Kindle e-reader launched on November 19, 2007 and sold out within hours despite a $399 price tag.
explanation: Its electronic ink display draws no power except when changing the image.

fact: E Ink technology was developed at MIT's Media Lab in the late 1990s and commercialized starting in 2004.
explanation: Its microcapsules contain charged white and black particles that move in response to electric fields.

fact: The first LCD display was developed at RCA in 1968 by a team led by George Heilmeier.
explanation: Commercial LCDs first appeared in calculators and digital watches in the early 1970s.

fact: The first OLED screens were commercialized in 1997 by Pioneer for a car stereo display.
explanation: OLED displays do not require backlights because each pixel emits its own light.

fact: The first commercial digital camera was the 1990 Dycam Model 1, also sold as the Logitech Fotoman, with 376x240 black-and-white pixels.
explanation: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson had built the first prototype digital camera in 1975.

fact: Kodak filed for bankruptcy in January 2012, in part because it failed to embrace the digital photography its own engineers had invented.
explanation: Sasson's 1975 prototype recorded a single black-and-white image to cassette tape in 23 seconds.

fact: Instagram was originally an iPhone-only check-in app called 'Burbn' before pivoting to photo sharing in 2010.
explanation: Co-founders Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger named it from 'instant camera' and 'telegram.'

fact: The first true smartphone, the IBM Simon, launched in 1994 and combined a cell phone with PDA features for $1,099.
explanation: It had a black-and-white touchscreen and supported email, fax, and a calendar.

fact: Pull-to-refresh, the gesture now common across apps, was patented by Loren Brichter, who originally designed it for the Tweetie iPhone app in 2008.
explanation: Twitter bought Tweetie in 2010 and licensed the pull-to-refresh patent for free use.

fact: The 'three-finger salute' (Ctrl-Alt-Delete) was created in the early 1980s by IBM engineer David Bradley as a hardware reset for the IBM PC.
explanation: Bradley joked at a public event that 'I may have invented it, but Bill made it famous.'

fact: The Blue Screen of Death first appeared in Windows 3.1 in 1992 and became iconic in Windows NT and 95.
explanation: Microsoft's Steve Ballmer wrote one early version of the 'Ctrl-Alt-Del' kernel screen text.

fact: The 'sad Mac' icon was displayed when classic Mac OS encountered a fatal startup error, often with an error code below.
explanation: It was replaced with the 'folder with a question mark' icon in later versions.

fact: The first widely used graphical web browser to support inline images was Mosaic 1.0 in 1993, developed primarily by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina.
explanation: Before then, images had to be opened in separate viewer applications.

fact: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) was proposed by Hakon Wium Lie in 1994 and standardized as CSS1 in 1996.
explanation: He worked at CERN at the time alongside Tim Berners-Lee.

fact: XML was developed as a simplification of SGML and was published as a W3C Recommendation in February 1998.
explanation: It became the basis for many data exchange formats including RSS and SOAP.

fact: JSON was popularized by Douglas Crockford in the early 2000s and standardized as ECMA-404 in 2013.
explanation: It is a subset of JavaScript object literal syntax and now serves as a default web data format.

fact: WebAssembly (Wasm), a portable binary code format for the web, was first released as a W3C standard in 2019.
explanation: It enables near-native execution speeds in modern browsers.

fact: The Apple I, designed entirely by Steve Wozniak in 1976, was sold for $666.66 and required users to add their own case, keyboard, and monitor.
explanation: Only about 200 were ever made, and surviving units now sell at auction for hundreds of thousands of dollars.

fact: The Apple II, released in 1977, was one of the first mass-produced personal computers with color graphics out of the box.
explanation: It remained in production until 1993 in some configurations.

fact: The Commodore 64, released in 1982, holds Guinness World Records for best-selling single computer model, with estimates between 12.5 and 17 million units.
explanation: Its name reflects its 64 KB of RAM.

fact: The Amiga 1000, released by Commodore in 1985, was a pioneering multimedia computer with multitasking and impressive graphics for its time.
explanation: Its graphical demos were used as a video-effects tool for early television production.

fact: Sinclair's ZX Spectrum, launched in 1982 in the UK, sold over 5 million units and helped launch the British games industry.
explanation: Its rubber-keyed keyboard inspired the affectionate British nickname 'Speccy.'

fact: Atari Inc. was founded in 1972 by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, with $250 each in startup capital.
explanation: The name comes from a term in the Japanese game Go meaning 'in a state of being threatened.'

fact: Atari paid Steve Jobs $750 to design a circuit board for Breakout in 1976; he gave Wozniak half of that and they completed the design in four days.
explanation: Jobs reportedly received a much larger bonus from Atari that he did not share with Wozniak.

fact: The Pixar Image Computer, originally part of Lucasfilm, was sold in 1986 to Steve Jobs for $5 million when it became Pixar.
explanation: Jobs invested another $5 million in working capital and would inject roughly $50 million more before Toy Story succeeded.

fact: Pixar's Toy Story (1995) was the first feature-length film made entirely with computer-generated imagery.
explanation: The animation team often rendered scenes overnight on hundreds of Sun workstations.

fact: Adobe Systems was founded in 1982 by John Warnock and Charles Geschke after they left Xerox PARC.
explanation: Steve Jobs offered to buy Adobe in 1982 for $5 million; the founders declined and went public a few years later.

fact: Hewlett-Packard was founded in 1939 in a Palo Alto garage by Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard with $538 in initial capital.
explanation: The garage is now designated 'the birthplace of Silicon Valley'.

fact: Silicon Valley was named in a 1971 series of articles by journalist Don Hoefler in Electronic News titled 'Silicon Valley USA.'
explanation: The 'silicon' refers to the material used in semiconductor manufacturing.

fact: The first commercial silicon transistor was produced by Texas Instruments in 1954, replacing the more fragile germanium transistors then in use.
explanation: Silicon offered better thermal stability and higher operating temperatures.

fact: The pocket calculator was popularized by Texas Instruments' Cal-Tech prototype in 1967 and Bowmar's 901B 'Brain' in 1971.
explanation: By 1980, electronic calculators were so cheap they were given away as advertising premiums.

fact: Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell, released in 1978, was one of the first consumer devices to use digital signal processing for speech.
explanation: Its TMS5100 chip used linear predictive coding to synthesize words.

fact: The Mac OS 'Happy Mac' icon greeted users at startup from 1984 until it was replaced in Mac OS X 10.2 in 2002.
explanation: It was designed by Susan Kare, who designed many of the original Macintosh icons.

fact: Susan Kare designed many original Macintosh icons including the Command symbol, which she adapted from a Swedish road sign for a campsite.
explanation: The symbol's official Unicode name is 'PLACE OF INTEREST SIGN.'

fact: The trash icon on the Macintosh was originally a regular wastebasket and changed shape in Mac OS X to a mesh design.
explanation: Apple was sued by trash bin maker United Industries in 1989 over alleged similarity to one of its designs.

fact: WordPerfect dominated the word processor market in the late 1980s before being overtaken by Microsoft Word during the early 1990s.
explanation: WordPerfect's slow transition to Windows is widely cited as a major reason for its decline.

fact: Lotus 1-2-3, the dominant spreadsheet of the mid-1980s, was eventually overtaken by Microsoft Excel after Excel launched on Windows in 1987.
explanation: IBM acquired Lotus in 1995 for about $3.5 billion.

fact: The first version of Microsoft Office, released in 1990, included Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.
explanation: PowerPoint had been acquired by Microsoft in 1987 from startup Forethought for $14 million.

fact: Microsoft's Clippy, the animated paperclip Office Assistant, debuted in Office 97 and was finally retired by default in Office 2007.
explanation: Time magazine listed Clippy among the 'worst inventions' of the twentieth century.

fact: The first emoji on Unicode arrived in version 6.0 of the standard in 2010, adding 722 emoji characters.
explanation: Apple's iOS 5 then exposed an emoji keyboard worldwide, accelerating global adoption.

fact: The OpenSSL library, used by a majority of secure websites in the 2010s, was maintained largely by a single full-time developer until after Heartbleed.
explanation: The Core Infrastructure Initiative was created in 2014 in response, with major tech companies funding maintenance.

fact: The original Mac's chime sound was created by jazz musician and Apple engineer Jim Reekes in 1991 and named 'Mac startup sound.'
explanation: Reekes designed it to be relaxing after he found previous chimes unpleasant.

fact: The 'Intel Inside' jingle, four notes used since 1994, is one of the most heard pieces of audio in history.
explanation: It was composed by Walter Werzowa to evoke 'innovation, troubleshooting and the inside of a computer.'

fact: The default Windows 95 startup sound was composed by Brian Eno on a Mac, despite Microsoft's PC focus.
explanation: Eno was paid $35,000 and instructed to produce something 'inspiring, universal, optimistic, futuristic.'

fact: The Nokia ringtone 'Nokia Tune' is an excerpt from a guitar piece called 'Gran Vals' written by Francisco Tárrega in 1902.
explanation: Nokia did not credit the source until years after the tone became its sonic logo.

fact: Apple's iconic 'Mac Mac' chime returned to MacBooks with macOS Big Sur in 2020 after being silenced on portable Macs for years.
explanation: The startup chime had been disabled by default starting with the 2016 MacBook Pro.

fact: The first computer animation in a feature film appeared in 1973's 'Westworld', showing a pixelated view of the world from a robot's perspective.
explanation: It was created using a 2D vector display and primitive scanning hardware.

fact: Tron, released in 1982 by Disney, was the first major Hollywood feature to use extensive computer-generated imagery for its environments.
explanation: It was disqualified from a special effects Oscar because the Academy thought computers were 'cheating.'

fact: Pixar's RenderMan software, used in nearly every major animated film since Toy Story, was first released in 1989.
explanation: It has been used in winners of more than 40 Academy Award for Visual Effects films.

fact: The Pentium FDIV bug, discovered in 1994, was a flaw in Intel's Pentium processor that caused certain floating-point divisions to return incorrect results.
explanation: Intel initially downplayed the problem but ultimately took a $475 million charge to replace affected chips.

fact: Intel's first commercial microprocessor, the 4004, was originally designed for a Japanese calculator company called Busicom.
explanation: Intel later bought back the rights to the chip from Busicom for $60,000.

fact: The first patent for an integrated circuit was issued to Jack Kilby in 1959 for his 'miniaturized electronic circuits.'
explanation: Robert Noyce's slightly later but more practical planar IC formed the basis of modern manufacturing.

fact: The Bell Labs vacuum tube, the predecessor to transistors, was invented around the early 1900s, with Lee de Forest patenting the triode in 1906.
explanation: Vacuum tubes powered early computers like ENIAC and most consumer electronics until the late 1950s.

fact: Hedy Lamarr, the Hollywood actress, co-invented a frequency-hopping technique in 1942 that helped lay the conceptual groundwork for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
explanation: She received the U.S. patent (with George Antheil) for a 'Secret Communication System' used to control torpedoes.

fact: The first commercial digital cellular phone call took place in 1991 in Finland using GSM technology.
explanation: Then-prime minister Harri Holkeri made the call to Helsinki's deputy mayor.

fact: Cell phones replaced car phones in popularity in the 1990s, after handheld units became small and cheap enough to carry.
explanation: By 2002, mobile phones outnumbered landline phones globally.

fact: The first cordless phone, the Carter Phone, was developed in the 1960s as an external connection between a two-way radio and the public phone network.
explanation: A 1968 FCC decision involving the Carter Phone helped open the U.S. phone market to non-AT&T equipment.

fact: Iridium 33 collided with the defunct Russian satellite Kosmos 2251 on February 10, 2009, in the first major accidental satellite collision.
explanation: It produced more than 1,800 trackable debris fragments in low Earth orbit.

fact: The Hubble Space Telescope's primary mirror had a famous spherical aberration of about 2.2 micrometers when launched in 1990.
explanation: A 1993 servicing mission installed corrective optics that restored full operational capability.

fact: James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021 and is positioned at the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
explanation: Its primary mirror is 6.5 meters across and made of 18 hexagonal beryllium segments coated with gold.

fact: The Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, became the most distant human-made object and entered interstellar space in 2012.
explanation: It still communicates with Earth using a 22.4-watt transmitter, less powerful than a refrigerator bulb.

fact: Voyager 1 and 2 each carry a Golden Record containing sounds, images, and music from Earth for potential extraterrestrial finders.
explanation: The records include greetings in 55 languages and music by artists ranging from Bach to Chuck Berry.

fact: The Pioneer plaque, attached to Pioneer 10 and 11, depicted a man, a woman, and a map of pulsars indicating Earth's location.
explanation: It was designed by Carl Sagan, Linda Salzman Sagan, and Frank Drake.

fact: The first artificial neural network was the Perceptron, built by Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell in 1957.
explanation: Rosenblatt's optimistic claims contributed to the first 'AI winter' when the perceptron's limits were exposed.

fact: The backpropagation algorithm for training neural networks was popularized in a 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams.
explanation: Similar ideas had been developed earlier by Paul Werbos in his 1974 PhD thesis.

fact: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award for foundational work on deep learning.
explanation: Their decades of work on neural networks helped enable the modern deep learning revolution.

fact: The transformer architecture, the foundation of modern large language models, was introduced in the 2017 Google paper 'Attention Is All You Need.'
explanation: The paper's eight authors went on to found or join multiple major AI companies.

fact: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, and Mustafa Suleyman and acquired by Google in 2014 for an estimated $400 million.
explanation: It is best known for AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and other reinforcement learning breakthroughs.

fact: DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 made a major breakthrough in protein structure prediction at the 2020 CASP14 competition.
explanation: By 2022, AlphaFold's predictions covered nearly every known protein structure.

fact: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives including Dario and Daniela Amodei.
explanation: Its flagship AI assistant is called Claude.

fact: The 'Eliza effect' refers to the tendency of users to attribute human-like understanding to simple computer programs.
explanation: It is named after Joseph Weizenbaum's 1960s ELIZA chatbot.

fact: Bell Labs was the birthplace of many fundamental technologies including the transistor, the laser, Unix, C, and information theory.
explanation: Its scientists have won at least nine Nobel Prizes.

fact: Claude Shannon's 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' founded the field of information theory.
explanation: Shannon also showed in 1937 that Boolean algebra could implement any logical relationship in electrical circuits.

fact: The bit (binary digit) as a unit was named by John Tukey in 1946.
explanation: Shannon then used 'bit' as the fundamental unit of information in his 1948 paper.

fact: The byte was named by Werner Buchholz at IBM in 1956 during the design of the IBM Stretch supercomputer.
explanation: Buchholz spelled it 'byte' instead of 'bite' to avoid accidental confusion with 'bit'.

fact: ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, was first published by ANSI in 1963 and uses 7 bits to represent 128 characters.
explanation: It was based partly on telegraph codes from the 1860s.

fact: Unicode 1.0 was published in 1991 and originally fit all characters in 16 bits; the standard now defines more than 154,000 characters across many scripts.
explanation: UTF-8, an encoding compatible with ASCII, dominates modern web content.

fact: UTF-8 was designed by Ken Thompson and Rob Pike in 1992, reportedly sketched on a placemat at a New Jersey diner.
explanation: It is now the encoding for more than 98% of web pages.

fact: Adobe Reader was originally called Acrobat Reader and was made freely downloadable in 1994 to help spread the PDF format.
explanation: Adobe charged for the full Acrobat authoring tool, which created PDFs.

fact: The 'QR code' was invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave for tracking vehicle parts on Toyota assembly lines.
explanation: Its name stands for 'Quick Response' code.

fact: Barcodes were patented in 1952 by Norman Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver, after Woodland was inspired by drawing Morse code dots and dashes into the sand.
explanation: The first commercial barcode scan, on a pack of Wrigley's gum, occurred in 1974 at a Marsh supermarket in Ohio.

fact: RFID technology has its roots in WWII 'Identification Friend or Foe' systems used to distinguish friendly aircraft from enemy ones.
explanation: Modern passive RFID tags can be smaller than a grain of rice.

fact: The first ATM was inaugurated by Barclays in London on June 27, 1967 and was operated by John Shepherd-Barron's invention.
explanation: Customers used special punched paper checks instead of plastic cards.

fact: The first magnetic stripe credit card was developed at IBM in the late 1960s by Ron Klein and IBM engineer Forrest Parry.
explanation: Parry's wife reportedly suggested using a clothes iron to attach the magnetic tape to the card.

fact: The first chip-and-PIN payment cards (EMV) were rolled out in France in the early 1990s, decades before the U.S. transitioned.
explanation: EMV stands for Europay, Mastercard, and Visa, the three companies that established the standard.

fact: Apple Pay launched on October 20, 2014 in the United States and uses tokenization for secure mobile payments.
explanation: Tokens replace card numbers with device-specific values that are useless if stolen.

fact: PayPal, founded in 1998 by Confinity and later merged with Elon Musk's X.com, was acquired by eBay in 2002 for $1.5 billion.
explanation: PayPal was spun off from eBay in 2015 and is now an independent public company.

fact: The 'PayPal Mafia' refers to former PayPal executives and engineers who went on to found or invest in major tech companies like Tesla, LinkedIn, and YouTube.
explanation: Members include Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, Reid Hoffman, Max Levchin, and others.

fact: LinkedIn was founded by Reid Hoffman and others in late 2002 and launched on May 5, 2003.
explanation: Microsoft acquired LinkedIn in 2016 for about $26.2 billion.

fact: Uber was founded in 2009 as 'UberCab' by Travis Kalanick and Garrett Camp.
explanation: The name was shortened to 'Uber' after a 2010 cease-and-desist from San Francisco transportation regulators.

fact: Airbnb was founded in 2008 by Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia, and Nathan Blecharczyk, who first rented out air mattresses in their San Francisco apartment.
explanation: Its name is short for 'Air Bed & Breakfast.'

fact: Spotify was founded in Sweden in 2006 by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon and launched publicly in October 2008.
explanation: It went public via direct listing on the NYSE in April 2018.

fact: Netflix was founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph and started as a DVD-by-mail service before launching streaming in 2007.
explanation: Blockbuster turned down a chance to buy Netflix for $50 million in 2000.

fact: Tesla Motors was founded in 2003 by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning; Elon Musk joined as chairman and led its Series A in 2004.
explanation: Musk officially became CEO in October 2008 during the financial crisis.

fact: The first Tesla Roadster, delivered in 2008, was based on the Lotus Elise chassis and could go from 0 to 60 mph in under four seconds.
explanation: A Tesla Roadster was launched into space aboard SpaceX's Falcon Heavy in February 2018.

fact: SpaceX was founded by Elon Musk in 2002 with the goal of reducing space transportation costs and making Mars colonization possible.
explanation: Its Falcon 9 became the first orbital-class rocket to land vertically and be reused.

fact: SpaceX's Falcon 1 became the first privately developed liquid-fuel rocket to reach orbit in September 2008 on its fourth attempt.
explanation: The company was nearly bankrupt before that flight succeeded.

fact: The Roomba robotic vacuum, released by iRobot in 2002, was based on military robotics research and used spiral-and-randomize cleaning patterns.
explanation: iRobot was founded in 1990 by MIT roboticists Colin Angle, Helen Greiner, and Rodney Brooks.

fact: Boston Dynamics' BigDog robot, funded by DARPA starting in 2005, used hydraulics to traverse rough terrain.
explanation: Its quieter electric successor Spot is now commercially available for inspection and security tasks.

fact: The first robot to be patented in the United States, Unimate, was deployed at a General Motors plant in 1961 to move die casts.
explanation: It was created by George Devol and Joseph Engelberger, the latter often called the 'father of robotics.'

fact: The Czech writer Karel Capek introduced the word 'robot' in his 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots).
explanation: The term derives from the Czech 'robota,' meaning forced labor.

fact: Isaac Asimov's 'Three Laws of Robotics' first appeared in the 1942 short story 'Runaround.'
explanation: Asimov later added a 'Zeroth Law' overriding the others in his Foundation novels.

fact: The Boston Computer Society, active from 1977 to 1996, was at one point one of the world's largest computer user groups, with about 31,000 members.
explanation: Steve Jobs gave one of his most famous public Mac demos to the BCS in 1984.

fact: The People's Computer Company, founded in 1972 in Menlo Park, helped popularize early personal computing through a newsletter and computer center.
explanation: Steve Wozniak and other Homebrew Computer Club members were influenced by its philosophy.

fact: The Homebrew Computer Club met starting in March 1975 in Menlo Park and was a key incubator for early personal computing.
explanation: Steve Wozniak debuted what would become the Apple I at one of its meetings.

fact: Bill Gates wrote his 'Open Letter to Hobbyists' in 1976 complaining about widespread copying of his Altair BASIC interpreter.
explanation: It was an early defense of paid commercial software at a time when hobbyists routinely shared code.

fact: The original IBM PC ran at 4.77 MHz and shipped with 16 KB of RAM, expandable to 256 KB.
explanation: It used the Intel 8088 microprocessor and cost about $1,565 in its base configuration.

fact: Compaq's portable computer in 1983 weighed 28 pounds and was a 'sewing-machine sized' IBM PC compatible.
