explanation: It carried the IBM PC clone industry to mainstream business adoption.

fact: The IBM PCjr, launched in 1984 with a chiclet keyboard, is widely considered one of IBM's most famous product failures.
explanation: IBM cut its losses on the PCjr by 1985.

fact: Microsoft Office for Mac actually preceded Office for Windows, with Excel debuting on the Mac in 1985 and Word for Mac in 1985 as well.
explanation: Excel was Microsoft's first major application to ship for Mac before Windows.

fact: Microsoft's first product was a version of BASIC for the Altair 8800, written largely by Bill Gates and Paul Allen in 1975.
explanation: They began developing it before they even had access to an Altair, using an Intel 8080 simulator running on a PDP-10.

fact: The original Microsoft Windows logo, used until 1992, was a four-color flag often called the 'Windows flag.'
explanation: Microsoft replaced it with a wave-like design in 2012 and a more flat tile design in Windows 8.

fact: The first World Wide Web server was a NeXT computer at CERN that, by 1991, ran the world's only website.
explanation: A note taped to it read 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'

fact: NeXT, the company Steve Jobs founded after leaving Apple in 1985, made the workstation used to create the World Wide Web.
explanation: Apple bought NeXT in 1997, which brought Jobs back as CEO and laid the foundation for Mac OS X.

fact: Mac OS X is built on the NeXTSTEP operating system, which itself was based on Unix and the Mach kernel.
explanation: Many Cocoa APIs still use the 'NS' prefix as a reminder of NeXTSTEP.

fact: Adobe and Apple co-developed PostScript, which led to Apple's LaserWriter and helped trigger the desktop publishing revolution.
explanation: Aldus Corporation's PageMaker, launched in 1985 on the Mac, made it accessible to non-technical designers.

fact: The Comic Sans typeface was designed in 1994 by Vincent Connare at Microsoft for a cartoon dog assistant in Microsoft Bob.
explanation: Connare based the letterforms on hand-lettering in comic books.

fact: The Arial typeface, shipped widely with Microsoft products, was designed in 1982 by Robin Nicholas and Patricia Saunders for Monotype as a Helvetica alternative.
explanation: Its metrics match Helvetica's so that documents render identically when fonts are substituted.

fact: The Times New Roman font was designed in 1931 by Stanley Morison and Victor Lardent for The Times newspaper in London.
explanation: It became a default font for Microsoft Word and many web browsers for decades.

fact: The 'lorem ipsum' filler text used in graphic design comes from a scrambled passage of Cicero's 'De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum' written in 45 BC.
explanation: Typographers have used variations of the passage since at least the 1500s.

fact: The first Macintosh shipping box famously featured the 'It works' moment in which the Mac drew its own face on screen.
explanation: Apple's Susan Kare designed the original 'happy Mac' icon for the moment.

fact: The original 1984 Macintosh's 'Welcome to Macintosh' message was recorded by Apple engineer Steve Jobs himself in some demos.
explanation: The Macintosh could speak greetings via the MacInTalk software released later that year.

fact: The Apple Lisa, released in 1983 at $9,995, was named after Steve Jobs's daughter Lisa Nicole Brennan, though officially marketed as a backronym.
explanation: Apple's official backronym was 'Locally Integrated Software Architecture.'

fact: The Macintosh trash icon was redesigned by Susan Kare based on a Soviet-era Russian wastebasket she observed in a magazine.
explanation: The original Mac UI also drew inspiration from kitchen and office artifacts.

fact: The first commercially successful word processor, Wang Word Processing System, debuted in 1976 and ran on dedicated hardware.
explanation: Wang Laboratories was a $3 billion company by the mid-1980s before declining against PC software.

fact: The 'Internet of Things' phrase was coined in 1999 by Kevin Ashton during a presentation at Procter & Gamble about RFID and supply chains.
explanation: Ashton co-founded MIT's Auto-ID Center in the early 2000s.

fact: The first internet-connected appliance was a Coke vending machine at Carnegie Mellon University in the early 1980s.
explanation: It reported inventory and temperature over the campus network.

fact: The first widely used pretty-printer for source code, B Pretty Printer, was developed in the 1970s for the B programming language.
explanation: B was a direct ancestor of C and was created by Ken Thompson at Bell Labs in 1969.

fact: GCC, the GNU Compiler Collection, was first released by Richard Stallman in 1987 as part of the GNU Project.
explanation: It now supports dozens of languages and processor architectures.

fact: The LLVM compiler infrastructure was started by Chris Lattner at the University of Illinois in 2000 and is now used by Apple's Clang compiler.
explanation: Lattner later led Swift's development at Apple.

fact: Swift, Apple's programming language for iOS and macOS, was announced at WWDC 2014 and made open-source in 2015.
explanation: It was designed in part to replace Objective-C as Apple's main language.

fact: Kotlin was first released by JetBrains in 2011 and became Google's preferred language for Android in May 2019.
explanation: It is fully interoperable with Java and runs on the Java Virtual Machine.

fact: The Eclipse integrated development environment was open-sourced by IBM in November 2001.
explanation: IBM had spent about $40 million developing it internally before releasing it to the community.

fact: Visual Studio Code, launched by Microsoft in 2015, is built on Electron and has become the most popular general-purpose code editor by some surveys.
explanation: Its source is open under the MIT license, although the released binaries include Microsoft customizations.

fact: Electron, a framework for building cross-platform desktop apps with web tech, was created at GitHub in 2013 to power the Atom editor.
explanation: Apps including Slack, Discord, and VS Code are built with Electron.

fact: Node.js, a server-side JavaScript runtime, was created by Ryan Dahl in 2009 to handle high-concurrency network applications.
explanation: It runs on Google's V8 JavaScript engine.

fact: React, a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, was created by Facebook engineer Jordan Walke and open-sourced in 2013.
explanation: It introduced concepts like the virtual DOM that influenced many other frameworks.

fact: Angular, originally AngularJS, was released by Google in 2010 and rewritten as Angular 2 in 2016.
explanation: It is widely used in enterprise web applications.

fact: Vue.js, a popular JavaScript framework, was created by former Google engineer Evan You in 2014.
explanation: It is one of the few major front-end frameworks not backed by a corporate sponsor.

fact: Docker, a containerization platform, was first released in March 2013 by Solomon Hykes and quickly transformed software deployment.
explanation: It was built on Linux kernel features like cgroups and namespaces.

fact: Kubernetes, the open-source container orchestration system, was released by Google in 2014 and is descended from Google's internal Borg system.
explanation: Its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'helmsman' or 'pilot.'

fact: OpenStack, an open-source cloud computing platform, was launched in 2010 by Rackspace Hosting and NASA.
explanation: It powers private clouds for companies and organizations including CERN and PayPal.

fact: The first Wi-Fi-equipped consumer device certified by the Wi-Fi Alliance was Apple's iBook in 1999.
explanation: Steve Jobs demonstrated it by carrying a working laptop through a hoop on stage.

fact: The Cisco Aironet line of Wi-Fi products grew out of Cisco's 1999 acquisition of Aironet Wireless Communications.
explanation: Aironet had previously been a major supplier of wireless gear for retail and warehouses.

fact: The Bluetooth name was suggested by Intel's Jim Kardach, who had read about Harald Bluetooth in a Viking history book.
explanation: The name was originally meant as a placeholder before marketing, but it stuck.

fact: The pixel was named in 1965 by Frederic C. Billingsley of JPL while writing about lunar spacecraft images.
explanation: It is short for 'picture element.'

fact: The first 1-megapixel digital camera sensor, the Kodak KAF-1300, was introduced in the 1986 Nikon SVC prototype.
explanation: Consumer 1-megapixel cameras did not become widely affordable until the late 1990s.

fact: Charge-coupled devices (CCDs), the imaging sensor behind early digital cameras and astronomy, were invented at Bell Labs in 1969.
explanation: Willard Boyle and George Smith shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work.

fact: CMOS image sensors, which dominate today's cameras and smartphones, became practical in the 1990s thanks to work at JPL and others.
explanation: They consume far less power than CCDs and integrate easily with the rest of the camera's electronics.

fact: The first 'megapixel' phone camera was widely cited as the 2002 Sanyo SCP-5300 sold by Sprint in the U.S.
explanation: The Sharp J-SH04 in 2000 had a 0.11-megapixel camera and is often called the first camera phone.

fact: Snapchat's 'My Eyes Only' password-protected feature was added in 2016 to allow private storage of Snaps.
explanation: The company introduced Memories on July 6, 2016, fundamentally changing its 'ephemeral' brand.

fact: Snapchat's filters and lenses were partly powered by the 2015 acquisition of Looksery, a Ukrainian computer-vision startup.
explanation: Looksery cost Snap about $150 million in cash and stock.

fact: Pokemon Go launched in July 2016 and reached 500 million downloads worldwide by the end of that year.
explanation: It was made by Niantic, a Google spinoff that had previously developed the AR game Ingress.

fact: The first commercial virtual reality headset, the Sega VR, was announced in 1991 but never released due to safety concerns.
explanation: Sega worried about consumers walking into walls while wearing it.

fact: Oculus VR was founded in 2012 by Palmer Luckey, raised over $2.4 million on Kickstarter, and was acquired by Facebook in 2014 for $2 billion.
explanation: Its consumer Rift CV1 headset shipped in March 2016.

fact: The Apple Newton MessagePad, released in 1993, popularized the term 'personal digital assistant.'
explanation: It was discontinued in 1998 after Steve Jobs returned to Apple.

fact: The first internet domain name registrar was Network Solutions, which had a monopoly on .com, .net, and .org registrations until 1999.
explanation: ICANN's introduction of competitive registrars dramatically lowered domain prices.

fact: ICANN, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, was established in 1998 to manage internet name and number assignments.
explanation: It transitioned away from U.S. government oversight in October 2016.

fact: The first 'cyber Monday' was identified by retailers in 2005 as a peak shopping day for online stores following Thanksgiving.
explanation: The term was coined in a Shop.org press release that year.

fact: eBay was founded in 1995 by Pierre Omidyar in his San Jose home; the first item sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83.
explanation: Omidyar reportedly contacted the buyer to make sure he understood it was broken; the buyer was a 'collector of broken laser pointers.'

fact: Craigslist began in 1995 as an email list maintained by Craig Newmark to inform friends about local events in San Francisco.
explanation: It transitioned to a website in 1996 and famously remained largely text-based for decades.

fact: Reddit was founded by Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian in 2005 as part of Y Combinator's first cohort.
explanation: It was acquired by Condé Nast in 2006 before being spun out as an independent company in 2011.

fact: Y Combinator, a major startup accelerator founded by Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris, and Trevor Blackwell, began in 2005 in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
explanation: Its alumni include Dropbox, Airbnb, Stripe, Reddit, and Twitch.

fact: Dropbox was founded by Drew Houston and Arash Ferdowsi in 2007 after Houston repeatedly forgot a USB drive on a bus.
explanation: Steve Jobs reportedly tried to buy Dropbox in 2009 but was turned down.

fact: Stripe was founded in 2010 by brothers Patrick and John Collison from Ireland, both Y Combinator alumni.
explanation: Its early API became known for being unusually easy to integrate compared to rivals.

fact: Twitch was launched in June 2011 as a spinoff of the Justin.tv site for live video streaming.
explanation: Amazon acquired Twitch in 2014 for about $970 million.

fact: Apple's Siri voice assistant launched on the iPhone 4S in October 2011 and was based on technology Apple acquired from SRI International earlier that year.
explanation: The underlying SRI project, CALO, was funded by DARPA.

fact: Amazon's Alexa, named after the Library of Alexandria, launched with the Echo speaker in November 2014.
explanation: Its 'wake word' detection runs entirely on-device.

fact: Google Assistant was unveiled at Google I/O 2016 and integrated into the Pixel phone and Google Home.
explanation: It evolved from Google Now, an earlier predictive search service launched in 2012.

fact: Cortana, Microsoft's voice assistant launched in 2014, was named after the AI character in the Halo video game series.
explanation: Microsoft retired Cortana from Windows 11 in late 2023.

fact: The original Google logo was designed in 1998 by co-founder Sergey Brin using GIMP.
explanation: Designer Ruth Kedar created its modern serif version in 1999, used for over 15 years.

fact: Google's first Google Doodle was a stick figure behind the second 'o' to indicate that the founders were attending the Burning Man festival in 1998.
explanation: It was made on the founders' homepage so users would know why they weren't fixing the site.

fact: Gmail launched on April 1, 2004 with a then-unheard-of 1 GB of free storage per user.
explanation: Many initially thought the announcement was an April Fool's joke.

fact: Google Maps launched in February 2005 as a desktop service, and its mobile version launched a few years later, partly through Google's acquisition of Where 2 Technologies.
explanation: Google Earth grew out of a separate acquisition, Keyhole Inc., in 2004.

fact: Google Street View was launched on May 25, 2007 with imagery from five U.S. cities.
explanation: Its cars have driven more than 10 million miles to capture imagery worldwide.

fact: Google bought YouTube in October 2006 for $1.65 billion in Google stock.
explanation: At the time, YouTube was less than two years old.

fact: Google's parent company Alphabet was created on October 2, 2015 to separate Google's core search and ads business from other ventures.
explanation: Larry Page became Alphabet's first CEO; Sundar Pichai took over Google.

fact: Facebook rebranded its parent company as Meta Platforms in October 2021 to emphasize its focus on virtual and augmented reality.
explanation: The Facebook social network kept its name, but the corporate parent shifted its identity.

fact: Twitter rebranded as 'X' under Elon Musk in July 2023, replacing its iconic bird logo with a stylized 'X.'
explanation: Musk had previously used 'X.com' for an online bank that merged into PayPal.

fact: Elon Musk completed his acquisition of Twitter in October 2022 for $44 billion.
explanation: He attempted to back out of the deal, but a Delaware court trial forced him to close.

fact: Google's first datacenter was a cluster of inexpensive Linux PCs known as 'corkboard' servers at Stanford.
explanation: It was held together by Velcro and cork board because the founders had no money for proper enclosures.

fact: Google's MapReduce paper, published in 2004, inspired Hadoop and many later 'big data' systems.
explanation: Hadoop was created at Yahoo by Doug Cutting and named after his son's stuffed elephant.

fact: Apache Spark, a faster successor to MapReduce, was developed at UC Berkeley's AMPLab and open-sourced in 2010.
explanation: It performs in-memory computation to speed up iterative workloads.

fact: Google's BigTable paper in 2006 inspired several open-source NoSQL projects, including HBase.
explanation: BigTable was originally used to store data for products like Google Earth and web indexing.

fact: Tor's hidden services, identified by .onion addresses, allow servers to operate without revealing their IP addresses.
explanation: They were originally meant to protect dissidents and journalists in repressive countries.

fact: Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging app, is developed by the nonprofit Signal Foundation founded by Moxie Marlinspike and others.
explanation: Its protocol is also used by WhatsApp, Skype, and Google Messages for default end-to-end encryption.

fact: The Signal protocol was originally called the Axolotl Ratchet and is based on the Double Ratchet algorithm developed by Trevor Perrin and Moxie Marlinspike.
explanation: It provides forward secrecy and post-compromise security.

fact: The Tor Project was founded as a nonprofit in 2006 to maintain the Tor anonymity network.
explanation: Receiving funds from many sources including the U.S. State Department, the EFF, and individual donors.

fact: The .onion top-level domain became an official IETF special-use domain in 2015 (RFC 7686).
explanation: It is the only TLD reserved specifically for an anonymity network.

fact: The Wikipedia logo is an unfinished globe composed of jigsaw puzzle pieces with letters from various scripts.
explanation: Its current design was created by Paul Stansifer in 2003 and updated by David Friedland in 2010.

fact: The Stanford NLP Group's GloVe model and Google's Word2Vec, both released around 2013-2014, helped popularize word embeddings for NLP.
explanation: These models map words into dense vector spaces capturing semantic relationships.

fact: ImageNet, a labeled image database started by Fei-Fei Li at Princeton in 2009, contains more than 14 million images and helped launch modern deep learning.
explanation: Its annual competition was a major proving ground for new neural network architectures.

fact: The first 'AI winter,' a sustained downturn in AI research funding, occurred between roughly 1974 and 1980.
explanation: It was triggered by the Lighthill Report in the UK and DARPA cuts in the U.S.

fact: The 'computer mouse' got its name because the wire trailing behind it looked like a tail.
explanation: Douglas Engelbart originally called it an 'X-Y position indicator for a display system' in his 1970 patent.

fact: Apple's iconic 'Think Different' ad campaign was launched in 1997 after Steve Jobs returned to the company.
explanation: The voiceover was originally recorded by Richard Dreyfuss; an alternate version was narrated by Steve Jobs himself.

fact: The first 1984 Macintosh commercial, directed by Ridley Scott, aired during Super Bowl XVIII and is widely considered the greatest Super Bowl commercial.
explanation: Apple's board originally wanted to scrap the ad, but Steve Jobs insisted it run.

fact: Apple's 'iMac' name was suggested by ad executive Ken Segall in 1998; Steve Jobs initially preferred 'MacMan.'
explanation: Segall later wrote about the decision in his book 'Insanely Simple.'

fact: The original iMac G3, released in 1998, came in 'Bondi Blue' and helped revive Apple after years of decline.
explanation: It was the first major consumer computer to drop floppy disks and serial ports in favor of USB.

fact: Apple ditched the floppy drive entirely with the iMac G3 in 1998, well ahead of the industry.
explanation: Some buyers initially balked, but USB drives quickly filled the gap.

fact: Apple removed the 3.5mm headphone jack from the iPhone with the iPhone 7 in 2016, calling the decision 'courage.'
explanation: Many competitors followed within a year or two.

fact: The Apple Watch, launched in April 2015, was Apple's first new product category since the iPad in 2010.
explanation: By 2019, Apple Watch was outselling the entire Swiss watch industry by units.

fact: The AirPods, launched in December 2016, helped popularize true wireless earbuds in the consumer market.
explanation: Apple's W1 chip simplified pairing between AirPods and Apple devices.

fact: The Apple Pencil for iPad Pro launched in November 2015 and uses Bluetooth alongside ultra-fast touch sensing for low-latency drawing.
explanation: It has tilt and pressure sensitivity for fine artistic control.

fact: iPad launched in April 2010 and sold one million units in 28 days, faster than the original iPhone.
explanation: Apple later released the iPad mini, iPad Air, and iPad Pro variants.

fact: The Microsoft Surface line of tablets and laptops launched in 2012; the original Surface RT was a commercial flop and led to a $900 million inventory writedown.
explanation: Later Surface Pro and Surface Laptop models became more successful.

fact: Microsoft's Xbox was released in November 2001, marking the company's serious entry into the console gaming market.
explanation: Its name is a contraction of 'DirectX Box,' referring to Microsoft's graphics API.

fact: Microsoft acquired ZeniMax Media, parent of Bethesda Softworks, for $7.5 billion in 2021.
explanation: It then announced a $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard, closing in 2023.

fact: The Xbox Kinect was at one point the fastest-selling consumer electronics device ever, selling 8 million units in 60 days after its November 2010 launch.
explanation: Its depth-sensing technology was based on hardware from Israeli company PrimeSense.

fact: The Nintendo Wii, released in 2006, popularized motion-controlled gaming and sold more than 100 million units.
explanation: Its motion-sensing remote, the Wii Remote, was sometimes thrown into TVs by overenthusiastic players.

fact: The Game Boy survived being damaged in the Gulf War; a Game Boy recovered from a barracks bombing still worked on display at a Nintendo World Store.
explanation: The unit was on display at Nintendo World in New York for years.

fact: Mario, Nintendo's mascot, was originally named 'Jumpman' in Donkey Kong (1981).
explanation: He was later renamed after Mario Segale, the landlord of Nintendo of America's warehouse.

fact: Sega's Sonic the Hedgehog mascot debuted in June 1991 to compete with Nintendo's Mario.
explanation: Sega chose Sonic over a yellow rabbit prototype because the hedgehog spin attack tested better.

fact: Niantic's Ingress (2012) and Pokemon Go (2016) helped establish location-based augmented reality games.
explanation: Pokemon Go grossed over $1 billion within seven months of launch.

fact: The first computer-generated television commercial aired in 1959 for Cleveland's Sohio gas stations.
explanation: Computer animation was still a major novelty in commercial broadcasting for years.

fact: Pixar's 'Luxo Jr.' (1986) was nominated for an Academy Award and made the lamp Pixar's mascot.
explanation: It was directed by John Lasseter, who later became Pixar's chief creative officer.

fact: The first computer-generated graphics in a major motion picture appeared in 1976's 'Futureworld,' a sequel to 'Westworld.'
explanation: Edwin Catmull's CGI hand and face from 1972 were also featured.

fact: Quake (1996) by id Software was the first true 3D first-person shooter and helped popularize hardware-accelerated graphics.
explanation: Its engine was widely licensed and inspired later titles like Half-Life.

fact: Doom, released by id Software in December 1993, was distributed largely as shareware and helped popularize online distribution.
explanation: Its engine could be modded extensively, leading to a vibrant fan community.

fact: Half-Life, released by Valve in November 1998, was acclaimed for its scripted storytelling and helped redefine first-person shooters.
explanation: It originally ran on a heavily modified version of the Quake engine.

fact: Counter-Strike began as a Half-Life mod by Minh 'Gooseman' Le and Jess Cliffe in 1999.
explanation: Valve hired both creators and turned Counter-Strike into a flagship esports title.

fact: The first 'esports' tournament is sometimes traced to the 1972 'Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics' at Stanford University.
explanation: Players competed for a year-long subscription to Rolling Stone magazine.

fact: League of Legends was launched by Riot Games in 2009 and grew into one of the biggest games in esports.
explanation: Riot was acquired by Chinese tech giant Tencent in 2011 and fully bought out in 2015.

fact: Dota 2's annual world championship 'The International' has had prize pools exceeding $40 million.
explanation: Much of the prize money comes from in-game purchases by the player community.

fact: The largest data center campuses, like those run by Google, Microsoft, and Meta, can each consume hundreds of megawatts of electricity.
explanation: Hyperscale data centers worldwide accounted for over 1% of global electricity use as of the early 2020s.

fact: Bitcoin mining used about 100 to 150 terawatt-hours of electricity per year by some estimates in the early 2020s, comparable to the energy use of small countries.
explanation: Ethereum's 2022 'Merge' switched it from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake, cutting its energy use by over 99%.

fact: The world's most powerful supercomputer measured by the Top500 list, Frontier at Oak Ridge National Lab, exceeded one exaflop in 2022.
explanation: That is one quintillion (10^18) floating-point operations per second.

fact: Cray-1, released in 1976 by Cray Research, achieved 160 megaflops and is iconic for its C-shaped design with built-in seats.
explanation: Its seats hid the power supplies and cooling for the system.

fact: Seymour Cray, often called the 'father of supercomputing,' designed many of the world's fastest computers from the 1960s through the 1980s.
explanation: He famously preferred to handle key design problems with pencil and graph paper.

fact: The first transatlantic packet-switched network connection was made in 1973 between ARPANET and University College London.
explanation: It was relayed through Norway's NORSAR seismic monitoring network.

fact: The Cerf-Kahn 1974 paper, which introduced TCP, is sometimes called the founding document of the internet.
explanation: It described a protocol that could handle communication between heterogeneous networks.

fact: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn received the 2004 Turing Award for their fundamental work on internet protocols.
explanation: They also received the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005.

fact: The first computer-to-computer chat program for general use was 'talk,' standard on Unix systems by the mid-1980s.
explanation: Real-time chat over the internet was popularized by IRC, created by Jarkko Oikarinen in 1988.

fact: AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) launched in 1997 and was a dominant chat client among American teens through the early 2000s.
explanation: AOL retired AIM on December 15, 2017.

fact: ICQ, released in November 1996 by Israeli company Mirabilis, popularized internet-wide instant messaging.
explanation: AOL acquired Mirabilis in 1998 for an estimated $407 million.

fact: MSN Messenger launched in 1999 and was rebranded as Windows Live Messenger in 2005 before being merged into Skype in 2013.
explanation: At its peak it had over 330 million active users.

fact: BlackBerry Messenger (BBM) helped popularize the read receipt on mobile messaging and once carried strategic importance during events like the 2011 London riots.
explanation: BlackBerry retired the consumer version of BBM in 2019.

fact: Discord launched in May 2015 initially as a chat platform for gamers but expanded to general communities.
explanation: It surpassed 150 million monthly active users by 2021.

fact: The 'TikTok' app launched internationally in 2017 after ByteDance merged it with Musical.ly, which it had bought for about $1 billion.
explanation: Its Chinese sister app Douyin had launched a year earlier in 2016.

fact: Tumblr was founded by David Karp and Marco Arment in 2007 and was sold to Yahoo for $1.1 billion in 2013.
explanation: Verizon later sold Tumblr to Automattic in 2019 for a reported $3 million.

fact: WordPress was released in 2003 by Matt Mullenweg and Mike Little as a fork of the b2/cafelog blogging tool.
explanation: It now powers a large share of the world's websites.

fact: The first podcast feeds appeared around 2003-2004, helped by Dave Winer's RSS extensions and Adam Curry's automation tools.
explanation: Apple added podcast support to iTunes in June 2005, dramatically expanding the medium.

fact: RSS, the syndication format that helped fuel early blogs and podcasts, was developed at Netscape and UserLand starting in 1999.
explanation: Multiple incompatible versions exist; Atom emerged as an IETF alternative.

fact: The Atom Syndication Format was published as RFC 4287 in December 2005 to resolve fragmentation in syndication formats.
explanation: It uses XML and is similar in capability to RSS.

fact: OAuth, the open standard for delegated access used by 'log in with Google' and similar buttons, was created in 2006-2007 by Blaine Cook and others.
explanation: OAuth 2.0 was published as RFC 6749 in 2012.

fact: TLS 1.0 was published as RFC 2246 in 1999 as a successor to Netscape's SSL 3.0.
explanation: TLS 1.3, the modern version, was published in 2018 as RFC 8446.

fact: Let's Encrypt, a free certificate authority operated by the nonprofit ISRG, launched in 2016 and now issues hundreds of millions of certificates.
explanation: It helped raise the percentage of HTTPS-encrypted web traffic dramatically.

fact: Cloudflare was founded in 2009 by Matthew Prince, Lee Holloway, and Michelle Zatlyn and serves a substantial fraction of internet web traffic.
explanation: Its origin was an anti-spam project called Project Honey Pot.

fact: The first commercial CDN (content delivery network), Akamai, was spun out of MIT in 1998 by Tom Leighton and Daniel Lewin.
explanation: Lewin was killed in the September 11, 2001 attacks while traveling on American Airlines Flight 11.

fact: The first Apple App Store launched on July 10, 2008 with about 500 apps; today the store hosts millions.
explanation: Developers have collectively earned hundreds of billions of dollars through the store.

fact: The Google Play store, originally called Android Market, launched in October 2008 alongside the first Android device.
explanation: It was rebranded as Google Play in March 2012.

fact: Apple's Mac App Store opened on January 6, 2011 and brought app-store-style distribution to desktop computers.
explanation: It now coexists with Apple's classic non-store software distribution model.

fact: The 'Big O' notation for describing algorithm complexity was introduced by Paul Bachmann in 1894 in a number theory textbook.
explanation: It was popularized in computer science by Donald Knuth starting in the 1970s.

fact: Donald Knuth's 'The Art of Computer Programming' has been in progress since 1962; the first volume was published in 1968.
explanation: Knuth offers a reward check to anyone who finds an error in the books.

fact: Knuth created the TeX typesetting system in the 1970s after he was unhappy with the typography of his books.
explanation: Its version numbers approach the value of pi (e.g., 3.14159...).

fact: The first peer-reviewed computer science journal, Communications of the ACM, began publication in 1958.
explanation: It is published by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM).

fact: The first computer programming textbook, often credited as Maurice Wilkes's 'The Preparation of Programs for an Electronic Digital Computer', was published in 1951.
explanation: Wilkes led the EDSAC computer project at the University of Cambridge.

fact: EDSAC, completed at Cambridge in May 1949, was one of the earliest stored-program computers and ran one of the earliest video games, OXO (a tic-tac-toe game).
explanation: OXO was created by A. S. Douglas in 1952 as part of his PhD thesis on human-computer interaction.

fact: Manchester Baby, the world's first stored-program computer to run a program, executed its first code on June 21, 1948 at the University of Manchester.
explanation: The program calculated the highest proper factor of 2^18 and ran for 52 minutes.

fact: The first commercial computer in the United States, UNIVAC I, was delivered to the U.S. Census Bureau on March 31, 1951.
explanation: It successfully predicted Eisenhower's 1952 presidential election landslide on live television.

fact: Grace Hopper coined the term 'compiler' in the early 1950s; her A-0 system in 1952 was one of the first.
explanation: She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously in 2016.

fact: Grace Hopper rose to the rank of rear admiral in the U.S. Navy and worked actively into her 70s.
explanation: A U.S. Navy guided missile destroyer, the USS Hopper, was named in her honor.

fact: John von Neumann's 1945 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC' described the stored-program architecture used by virtually all modern computers.
explanation: The 'von Neumann architecture' separates memory from the CPU and treats programs as data.

fact: Alonzo Church's lambda calculus, developed in the 1930s, is a foundational model of computation equivalent in power to Turing machines.
explanation: It heavily influenced functional programming languages like Lisp and Haskell.

fact: Haskell, a purely functional programming language, was first released in 1990 and is named after logician Haskell Curry.
explanation: Its lazy evaluation model is distinctive among popular languages.

fact: Erlang, designed by Joe Armstrong and others at Ericsson in 1986, was created for telecommunications and is famous for its 'let it crash' fault tolerance.
explanation: It powered the AXD301 telephone switch with reported 99.9999999% availability.

fact: Elixir, built on the Erlang virtual machine, was created by José Valim and first released in 2011.
explanation: It is used in real-time and high-concurrency web systems, notably by Discord.

fact: The Scala programming language, designed by Martin Odersky and released in 2003, runs on the Java Virtual Machine.
explanation: Twitter migrated significant parts of its backend from Ruby to Scala in the early 2010s.

fact: Clojure, a Lisp dialect for the JVM, was created by Rich Hickey and first released in 2007.
explanation: It is known for emphasizing immutability and persistent data structures.

fact: F#, a functional-first language for .NET, was designed at Microsoft Research by Don Syme starting in 2002.
explanation: It is heavily influenced by OCaml.

fact: The OCaml programming language was developed by Xavier Leroy and colleagues at INRIA in France starting in 1996.
explanation: Facebook's Hack language and Jane Street's trading infrastructure are heavy users of OCaml.

fact: Dropbox famously wrote its desktop client in Python and used 'Pyston' and other tools to optimize Python performance.
explanation: Many other companies similarly built large-scale systems in Python despite its interpreter overhead.

fact: JetBrains, the company behind IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, and other IDEs, was founded in Prague in 2000 by three Russian developers.
explanation: Its IDEs are widely used by professional Java, Python, and other developers.

fact: Vim, a powerful text editor, was released by Bram Moolenaar in 1991 as an extension of the older Vi editor.
explanation: Donations to its development support the ICCF Holland charity for Ugandan children.

fact: Emacs was originally developed in 1976 by Richard Stallman and colleagues at MIT as an editor with a built-in Lisp interpreter.
explanation: GNU Emacs is one of the longest continuously developed software projects in history.

fact: The 'editor wars' between Vim and Emacs users have been a long-running joke in programming communities since at least the 1980s.
explanation: Some developers facetiously cite their editor choice as a religious affiliation.

fact: Microsoft's Internet Explorer was bundled into Windows starting in 1995, sparking the U.S. antitrust case against the company.
explanation: The 2001 settlement required Microsoft to share APIs with third-party software makers.

fact: The 2001 Microsoft antitrust case settlement reshaped how Microsoft was allowed to bundle software and integrate Internet Explorer with Windows.
explanation: Microsoft had been ordered split in two by Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson in 2000, but the order was overturned on appeal.

fact: The European Union has fined Google more than $9 billion across multiple antitrust cases since 2017.
explanation: The cases involved Google Shopping, Android, and AdSense advertising practices.

fact: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 public DNS service, launched on April 1, 2018, is one of the most widely used free DNS services in the world.
explanation: It is run jointly with the APNIC research project.

fact: Google's 8.8.8.8 public DNS launched on December 3, 2009 and became one of the most heavily used recursive DNS servers in the world.
explanation: It is anycast across many Google data centers globally.

fact: The first BBS (Bulletin Board System), CBBS, was created by Ward Christensen and Randy Suess in Chicago in February 1978.
explanation: BBSes were the predecessor to modern online communities and forums.

fact: Usenet, an early distributed discussion system, was created in 1979 by Duke University students Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis.
explanation: It originally used UUCP over telephone lines before migrating to the internet.

fact: The first .org domain was MITRE.org, registered on July 10, 1985.
explanation: MITRE is a U.S. nonprofit research organization.

fact: The first .edu domain was berkeley.edu, registered on April 24, 1985 by the University of California at Berkeley.
explanation: Educational domains are now limited to accredited U.S. higher education institutions.

fact: The dot-com bubble peak occurred in March 2000 when the NASDAQ Composite reached 5,048; it lost more than 75% of its value over the next 2.5 years.
explanation: Roughly 50% of dot-com companies created during the boom had vanished by 2004.

fact: Pets.com, an infamous dot-com era failure, spent millions on a Super Bowl ad in 2000 and went out of business about nine months later.
explanation: Its sock-puppet mascot survives in popular culture as a symbol of the bubble.

fact: Webvan, an online grocery startup, raised about $800 million from investors before filing for bankruptcy in July 2001.
explanation: It famously planned a national rollout before its operations had proven sustainable in any market.

fact: The first mass-produced 3D printer for consumers, the MakerBot Replicator, was released in 2012.
explanation: Most 3D printer designs descend from the open-source RepRap project started by Adrian Bowyer in 2005.

fact: Stereolithography, the foundational 3D printing process, was invented by Chuck Hull in 1983 and patented in 1986.
explanation: Hull co-founded 3D Systems, which is still a leading additive manufacturing company.

fact: The first publicly known printed firearm, the 'Liberator' single-shot pistol by Defense Distributed, was demonstrated in May 2013.
explanation: It prompted ongoing legal and regulatory debates over distributable firearm designs.

fact: The first commercial drone consumer product widely sold, the Parrot AR.Drone, debuted at CES 2010 controllable by Wi-Fi from an iPhone.
explanation: DJI later came to dominate the consumer drone market with its Phantom series.

fact: DJI was founded in 2006 in Shenzhen by Frank Wang and grew into the largest consumer drone maker in the world.
explanation: It captures a majority share of the global civilian drone market.

fact: The Mars rover Curiosity landed on Mars on August 6, 2012, using the novel 'sky crane' landing system.
explanation: Its mission was originally planned for two years but it remains operational over a decade later.

fact: Ingenuity, a NASA helicopter that arrived on Mars with the Perseverance rover, became the first powered aircraft to fly on another planet on April 19, 2021.
explanation: It completed more than 70 flights before its rotor was damaged in January 2024.

fact: The Mars Pathfinder Sojourner rover, which landed on Mars in 1997, was the first wheeled robotic vehicle to operate on another planet.
explanation: It weighed only 10.6 kilograms and traveled about 100 meters during its 83-day mission.

fact: Microsoft acquired Nokia's mobile phone business in 2014 for about $7.2 billion, then wrote down the value of the acquisition by $7.6 billion the following year.
explanation: It marked the end of Windows Phone as a competitive mobile operating system.

fact: Symbian, once the world's leading smartphone OS, was used in many Nokia phones and was open-sourced in 2010 before being discontinued in 2014.
explanation: At its peak in 2008, Symbian had around half of the smartphone market.

fact: The first commercial 5G networks launched in South Korea on December 1, 2018 by SK Telecom, KT and LG U+.
explanation: Verizon launched the first U.S. 5G service in select cities in April 2019.

fact: The world's first 4G LTE network was launched in Stockholm and Oslo by TeliaSonera on December 14, 2009.
explanation: It offered theoretical speeds up to 100 Mbit/s, much faster than 3G.

fact: Verizon was the first U.S. carrier to offer commercial 4G LTE service, launching on December 5, 2010.
explanation: Earlier 4G branded services like WiMAX from Sprint were not formally part of the LTE standard.

fact: The first commercial 3G network, launched by NTT DoCoMo in Japan in October 2001, used the W-CDMA standard.
explanation: It enabled mobile video calls, faster internet, and the spread of camera phones.

fact: The first cellular generation, 1G, used analog signals and was deployed broadly starting with NMT in the Nordic countries in 1981.
explanation: AMPS in the U.S. and TACS in the UK followed similar analog standards.

fact: The first text message in the U.S. is widely attributed to Vodafone-era messaging in the early 1990s, with carriers fully supporting SMS by 1995.
explanation: By 2003, U.S. consumers were sending billions of SMS messages per month.
